articles.title: Amazon threatens to leave NYC again, this time over delivery bill, as it rallies customers to fight it
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Amazon and New York City are fighting again.

The Seattle tech giant is threatening to move its delivery operations out of the city over a proposed law that would require it to directly employ the drivers who bring packages to New Yorkers’ doors. It’s also asking its customers to help fight the bill.

The legislation, known as the Delivery Protection Act or Intro 518 , would apply to companies that run last-mile delivery facilities in the city. Amazon is the main target, but FedEx and several regional couriers would also be covered.
Companies would need a license from the city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, which would also investigate complaints. The bill was introduced in February.

On Thursday, Amazon began showing New York City customers pop-up messages and a homepage banner that reads, “NYC Council could add up to $5 per order. Act now to protect low prices.” The notices link to a form and a pre-written letter customers can send to their council members to oppose the bill, Bloomberg reported . Amazon pointed GeekWire to a study by consulting firm AKRF estimating the bill would raise consumer costs by $409 to $664 a year, but didn’t detail how it arrived at the per-order figure.

In a blog post , Amazon said it relies on a network of small delivery businesses in the city. “If this legislation passes, we’d no longer be able to work with them, and we’d be forced to consider moving our operations outside of the city,” the company wrote. “That would likely mean slower and more expensive delivery for millions of customers in New York City, while also threatening small businesses and their thousands of employees.”

Amazon launched its Delivery Service Partners program in 2018, letting entrepreneurs start their own companies to deliver Amazon packages in Amazon-branded vans and uniforms. The companies hire their own drivers, while Amazon pays them to deliver and offers discounts on vehicles, fuel and insurance. The model lets Amazon expand its delivery network without directly employing drivers.

In a statement to GeekWire, Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel said the bill “as written” would threaten more than 40 small delivery businesses the company works with in the city and the more than 5,000 New Yorkers they employ. More than 2,000 Amazon employees also work at its delivery facilities in the city, the company said.

“We’re hopeful this bill doesn’t pass as written,” Nantel said. “But so far, key City Council members seem uninterested in learning about our delivery operations.” Amazon said neither Council Member Tiffany Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, nor Mayor Zohran Mamdani has accepted its offer to visit a delivery facility. The company also said customers sent about 20,000 emails to council members within six hours of the campaign’s launch Thursday morning.

The standoff echoes Amazon’s 2019 reversal on its second headquarters. That February, the company abruptly canceled plans to build a 25,000-person “HQ2” office in Long Island City, Queens, after more than a year of competition among cities to host it. Amazon blamed “a number of state and local politicians” who opposed the project, which drew fierce criticism over roughly $3 billion in government incentives.

Amazon stuck with its plans for Arlington, Va., and Nashville and didn’t reopen its search. Polls at the time showed most New Yorkers supported the deal, but Queens officials, labor leaders and activists fought it. State Sen. Michael Gianaris, who led the opposition, accused Amazon of trying to shake down governments to get its way.

City leaders backing the delivery bill see a familiar pattern. “Amazon is once again making spurious attacks against this commonsense legislation that would make workers and our streets safer,” said Cabán, the bill’s sponsor, who called Amazon’s warning a “dishonest scare tactic.”
City Council Speaker Julie Menin questioned Amazon’s cost claims in a post on X .

“It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers’ cost of living if it’s forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections,” she wrote, adding that the council is “crafting legislation that regulates Amazon and protects workers, without impacting prices or jobs.”

Mamdani endorsed the bill in August, saying Amazon’s subcontractor model “leaves workers vulnerable and corporations free to avoid accountability for reckless conditions on city streets,” CNBC reported .

Supporters, including the Teamsters union, which has sought to organize Amazon drivers and warehouse workers, say the bill would make the work safer and make it harder for Amazon to distance itself from driver injuries.

Amazon disputes that the bill would improve safety. The company said it has invested more than $2.5 billion in driver safety since 2019, that the serious crash rate for its drivers in New York City fell 35.7% from 2024 to 2025, and that drivers there have averaged nearly $24 an hour since January 2025, with required health coverage and paid time off.
Meanwhile, business groups have run ads against the bill and warned they may sue the city if it passes, according to CNBC . The measure is awaiting review by Menin.

articles.title: So you got a Microsoft Voluntary Exit Offer? Here’s what to do next
articles.author: Nikesh Parekh
paras: Nikesh (Niki) Parekh is a former Microsoft GM who is now CEO of Seattle-based AI talent recruiting startup Provn. This is the fourth post in his series on “Life after Big Tech,” including the Seattle startup guide , laid off at 50 and VC funding is changing dramatically .
Tens of thousands of Microsoft employees have a big decision to make in the next few weeks: take the company’s offer to leave, or stay and take their chances.

Microsoft chief people officer Amy Coleman announced the initiative in a memo on Oct. 26: a Voluntary Exit Offer (VEO) for about 60,000 employees at level 70 and below, which includes general managers and some vice presidents, in the U.S., Canada, the U.K. and India. That’s roughly 27% of Microsoft’s 223,000 people. The company expects 3,000 or fewer of them to accept .

Microsoft says the terms match its standard severance: base pay tied to level and tenure, continued stock vesting, a period of health coverage and career transition help. The severance package varies greatly based on the seniority or level of the employee and the number of years of service. Employees have until early December to decide and would leave by the end of the year.
The offer follows the Voluntary Retirement Program (VRP) that Microsoft extended to about 8,750 U.S. employees in April. About 30% of them, or roughly 2,600 people, took that offer.

All of this comes as Microsoft cuts jobs and changes the kinds of roles it hires for, while pouring money into AI infrastructure and data centers. At the same time, AI is reshaping the broader workforce, flattening management layers and changing what employers look for in new hires.
The worry I hear most is whether more layoffs are waiting on the other side. So the real choice is whether you leave on your own terms or let the company decide for you.
I hear two questions from Microsoft employees thinking about the VEO: How easily can I get another job, and how hard is it to start a company right now?
Harder than you think, and it depends a lot on who you are. We are in the “low hire, low fire” economy.
There is MASSIVE demand for AI-native builders — product managers, data scientists and engineers — as companies adapt products to deal with AI. Companies are also in the process of adopting AI.

One of the fastest-growing tech roles is the “Forward Deployed Engineer,” who implements AI solutions at customers. Security is also job #1 as models and agents get smarter and better at hacking legacy systems.

But it is very hard to be seen by recruiters and hiring managers right now. Candidates are using AI to customize their resumes to each job and using AI agents to apply, sending out 100 to 200 job applications per day. Recruiters are inundated with resumes and job applications, many of which are fake or inappropriate for the role.
It is critical to leverage your network in the job search, which can be hard if you have spent your entire career within one company.

Hiring managers have changed what they look for, too. AI fluency is becoming table stakes. The “process” of how you build/sell/market with AI is more important than what you build. Candidates are expected to show prototypes and proof of how they use AI tools every day.
The jobs themselves are changing. A friend told me last month that he wanted an engineering manager role. There are fewer manager roles in the market now.

AI has driven a reduction in management layers and a general flattening of organizations. The engineering team at a small AI company today is a CTO and a group of strong individual contributors. It is normal for managers to have 10 to 30 direct reports now, versus five to 10 in the pre-AI era.
Product management, program management and design teams are shrinking, as well, as AI automates certain jobs.

Hiring managers may view spending your whole career at Microsoft as a yellow flag. Microsoft is an iconic but unusual company. Almost no one else sells to and services customers the way Microsoft does, with an account executive inside nearly every large enterprise in the world.
The skills that get you promoted in Redmond don’t always carry over to a 500- to 5,000-person software company.
It has never been easier to build a product, and it has rarely been harder to fund a company.
Software is cheap to build now. A product leader and an engineer using AI tools can ship in weeks what used to take a team a year.
This cuts both ways for startups. Every good idea attracts a dozen competitors within months, and the big platforms will copy anything that works.

The true strength of a startup today is the ability to grow revenue quickly and establish leadership in a beachhead market. The sales, marketing, product-led growth and distribution strategies are becoming the most critical parts of the business.

The bar for venture funding is extremely high. Jason Lemkin of SaaStr recently shared data from ICONIQ showing that top “AI forward” startups under $10 million in annual recurring revenue are growing 900% a year at the median.

One venture investor told me they advise their portfolio companies that if they aren’t on track for a $10 million run rate within two years, they won’t raise another round. Last week I spoke with an investor who owns part of a business with $4 million in revenue, growing 100% a year and losing $1 million, and it can’t raise.

1) Think VERY big, raise a lot and grow fast enough to justify it. Build an incredible team pursuing an ambitious idea. Raise a large round based on the promise of becoming the next Anthropic, OpenAI or legal AI startup Harvey. Many of the most interesting companies are not software or AI-related, but are “deep tech” companies in defense, robotics, energy and biotech.

2) Raise a moderate amount of money from angels, family offices and nontraditional funds to build a business that has the ability to be profitable on one round of financing. You can control your destiny by building a company that doesn’t rely on the venture capital funding market.
3) Bootstrap and build a business that you own. Fund it yourself, grow it with revenue and get to profitability.
The question that most people are NOT asking is: What do I really want?
Before December, block out an afternoon and think about the last time you were happy at work.

There are many frameworks for figuring out what you want in your career and life in general. I’m a fan of the Four Elements exercise . Write down three times in your career when you felt energized and effective. From those, work out what gives you energy, where you have the most impact, what culture you do best in and what your constraints are: money, kids, aging parents and how many more years you want to work.
On LinkedIn, I have seen examples of Microsoft employees taking the VEO to start their own businesses in property management, buy car washes, take time to recharge, spend time with family and travel.
Other employees are starting the job search in earnest but not taking the VEO. Many others are just getting back to work and doubling down on Microsoft.

Whichever way you go, start now. Start by aligning on your priorities and what you want from your career. If you stay, use the next year to build your skills with AI and to grow a network outside Redmond. If you leave to build something, decide early which of the three funding paths you’re on, because that choice shapes everything that follows.

The people I’ve watched land well after Big Tech had one thing in common: they knew what they wanted before they walked out the door, whether that was a new role, a company of their own or a year with their family.

articles.title: Uncommon Thinkers: Andrew Redd’s audacious plan to turn ocean volcanoes into power plants
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners .

Andrew Redd ‘s career path creates a tidy narrative: grow up in Seattle steeped in aviation and maritime culture, study mechanical engineering and aerospace, work at SpaceX, then launch an offshore geothermal energy startup.
The dots connect, but the picture they form is anything but ordinary: bold in vision, fast in execution and enormous in potential.

Redd has next-level ambition, and he’s directing it at solving one of the world’s biggest and most urgent problems — adding renewable, massively scalable energy that can outcompete fossil fuels and reach the grid quickly enough to make a difference in the race against climate change.
Underwater geothermal energy has never been tapped in a significant way, but to Redd, the idea was irresistible. “It checks all of the boxes for our perfect future energy source,” he said.

He founded Endurance Energy on the north shore of Seattle’s Lake Union in January 2025, and this September the team oversaw its fifth deep-sea deployment. At a site 300 miles off the Oregon coast, its prototype system generated more electricity than it consumed. The startup has raised $63 million from investors and has roughly three dozen employees.
Nate Bek , a principal at Ascend, praised Redd’s ability to attract “brilliant” talent in pursuit of his goal. The Seattle venture firm is one of the startup’s early backers.

“I’ve been deeply inspired by what [Redd]’s building at Endurance and haven’t shut up about it since the day we met,” Bek said. “He somehow makes powering the world from the bottom of the ocean feel inevitable, all while remaining remarkably measured and transparent about the progress.”

For Redd, studying engineering and aerospace in college was so clear-cut that it wasn’t a choice at all. Growing up around Boeing, seaplanes, the Museum of Flight and the Pacific Northwest’s rich maritime industry naturally pointed him toward those sectors. He wanted a degree as expansive as his influences.
“I didn’t really want to have to choose whether it was going to be boats or space travel or airplanes,” he said. “I just wanted to be able to do anything — keep the world as wide open as possible.”

After graduating from Princeton University, Redd worked at Neuralink, an Elon Musk company developing technology that lets the brain communicate directly with computers. A year later, in 2021, he moved to Musk’s rocket company, SpaceX.
That was another no-duh decision, as Redd viewed it.

“I saw SpaceX as really the place to be, where early-career people are given the most amount of resources and responsibility, and that felt like the fastest way to learn and the most engaging possible scenario to be in,” Redd said. “I wanted to be tossed into something that was a little bit crazy.”

Redd joined as SpaceX was starting to build its first orbital Starship rockets. The program brought together passionate young people and experienced SpaceX engineers who served as mentors. Wild ideas were entertained and explored. Everyone was committed to the mission. It was just the experience Redd wanted, and he planned to stick around for seven to 10 years.
Then artificial intelligence started booming.

In 2024, the build-out of sprawling, energy-hungry data centers for AI was accelerating with no end in sight. At the same time, efforts to electrify transportation, heating and cooling were driving up demand for power. Redd saw these trends sparking a surge in new natural gas generation, locking in decades of carbon emissions.

He wanted to find a better way. He went into engineering mode, focusing on all the essential criteria for an energy source: it had to be clean, not dependent on intermittent sun or wind, capable of producing massive amounts of energy, readily deployable, subject to fewer regulatory hurdles than something like nuclear, economically competitive, and scalable.

Redd recognized the tremendous heat contained under Earth’s surface as a terrific source for renewable energy and realized that most of the world’s active volcanoes are offshore. The unknown was whether the rocky ocean floor would be suitable for geothermal wells, so he did some research and found publications from geology experts who said the conditions would be “perfect.”

“You can tell,” he said, “when there’s a moment in time that you need to go and reach out and grab something, and that was really my impression — if I didn’t start this now, this would never come into existence, or wouldn’t come into existence soon enough to make a meaningful impact.”

In launching Endurance, Redd was intentional about the culture he wanted to create. He was aiming for a multidisciplinary group of mission-driven employees eager to collaborate and learn from each other: top talent that would attract more of the same and make Endurance a place people were excited to work.
“The hardest part of an early-stage startup is recruiting,” Redd said, “especially if you’re a first-time founder.”
The startup employs about a dozen SpaceX alumni, plus employees from the fusion company Helion Energy and the aerospace venture Blue Origin.

A strong team is key to Endurance’s success. That’s because, enthusiasm and passion aside, the startup faces steep engineering and economic challenges. The technology must withstand high pressure, corrosive conditions and mineral scaling inside devices, and seafloor machinery could be costly to repair. The systems will need expensive subsea cables to carry power to shore over potentially long distances. It’s a heavy lift.

While the September sea trial didn’t go perfectly, Redd is happy with the results. The company landed its 3-ton power plant on the seafloor near a natural vent and produced net energy from it — albeit for only 8.7 seconds. Technical difficulties and a power-cable failure cut the dive short.

Team members successfully operated the system remotely from Seattle through a fiber-optic network running along the seabed. Redd said he’s grateful for access to the network, which is part of the National Science Foundation’s Regional Cabled Array and operated by the University of Washington.

Endurance engineers also drilled what they called the world’s first subsea geothermal well at a site about 5,000 feet below the ocean’s surface. The 2-inch-wide, 52-foot-deep well delivered hydrothermal fluid, but the flow was too restricted to run the power plant, sending the team to the natural vent.
Redd said there’s a lot of work ahead, but the team “made huge strides” in learning and in reducing the project’s risks.

The company now is developing Leopard, its 2-megawatt generator. After testing the technology at the research site off the Oregon coast, Endurance aims to deliver power from a Leopard system in Tonga next year as its first commercial project. Subsea geothermal energy could ultimately reduce the island nation’s reliance on imported diesel and put the startup one step closer to its objective of generating terawatts of planet-friendly energy.
“This was always the end goal,” Redd said. “Create something that is highly meaningful for the world.”
Editor’s Note: Nate Bek of Ascend is a former GeekWire reporter.

articles.title: Amazon’s $18B bet on Anthropic tops $200B, for a moment, in the Claude maker’s historic market debut
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: Anthropic made its Nasdaq debut today in a record $81.3 billion initial public offering , with big financial stakes for the Seattle area’s two tech giants.

For Amazon, the IPO is a paper windfall. The company started putting money into Anthropic in 2023, about $18 billion in all . At the $83 IPO price, its stake was worth about $161 billion . With Anthropic opening at $111.50 a share, that number was closer to $216 billion. The stock has since dropped below $100, which put Amazon’s stake under $200 billion.
Beyond the value of the investment, Anthropic is a major customer for Amazon’s cloud platform. The Claude maker has committed to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon Web Services through 2036.

For Microsoft, it’s more complicated. The Redmond company agreed in late 2025 to invest up to $5 billion but hasn’t disclosed the size of its stake. Microsoft is buying $1 billion of Anthropic stock alongside the IPO, one of seven tech companies buying a combined $26 billion. Anthropic has committed to spend at least $47 billion on Microsoft’s Azure cloud through 2033.
But Microsoft is also pitching its own AI models against Anthropic’s, and it has been working to replace Anthropic’s models with OpenAI’s in some Copilot features, The Information reported this week.

Listing Anthropic’s compute partners on CNBC this morning , co-founder Daniela Amodei named Nvidia, Amazon, Google and Broadcom, but not Microsoft. Whether it was a slip or something more significant, it was an interesting omission.
A historic debut: The offering tops SpaceX’s $75 billion IPO in June, and it makes Anthropic the first standalone AI lab to go public, ahead of OpenAI.

The five-year-old company was valued at about $1.5 trillion at the $83 IPO price, on a fully diluted basis that counts employee stock and other shares not yet issued. The stock opened at $111.50 , valuing Anthropic at about $2 trillion on the same basis. It has since traded as low as about $95 .

Speaking before the opening bell, CEO Dario Amodei said Anthropic will slow the training and release of its AI models for as long as it takes to be confident they’re safe, and that going public only strengthens that resolve.
“We will not bend to either business nor political pressure,” he said.
In an interview with CNBC’s Andrew Ross Sorkin afterward, Amodei called the push and pull between growth and that kind of restraint “one of the central tensions at the heart of the company.”
Anthropic is also a public benefit corporation, a structure that legally requires the company to balance shareholders’ interests with the public good.
What’s next: Both Seattle-area giants have hedged their bets. Microsoft owns about 24% of OpenAI , and Amazon put $50 billion into OpenAI earlier this year.
OpenAI, which confidentially filed for its own IPO in June, is still aiming to go public in 2027.
Anthropic’s co-founders and some of its biggest shareholders are barred from selling for up to a year under the IPO’s lock-up rules, and Amazon has said it expects a customary lock-up period.

Amazon will update the value of its Anthropic holdings in its fourth-quarter results, much of it through earnings, which means the paper windfall is likely to boost Amazon’s fourth-quarter profit even though it hasn’t sold a share.

articles.title: Zeno Power makes progress on an underwater power system that will eventually go nuclear
articles.author: Alan Boyle
paras: Zeno Power has hit a major milestone in its push to build nuclear batteries for underwater use.

The startup said today that it successfully demonstrated an electrically heated Stirling generator in a controlled maritime setting in Washington state. The two-week demonstration produced electrical power outputs in excess of 20 watts, said Lindsey Boles, Zeno’s chief product officer.

“It’s a really big step for us — just solidifying our expertise in how to design these, and then confirming our ability to translate that into operational hardware that meets or exceeds what our customers need,” Boles told GeekWire.

Zeno is developing the power system with support from the Department of Defense as a follow-up to an initial $7.5 million contract awarded in 2023. The generator uses a Stirling engine to convert heat into electricity by cycling gas through heating and cooling phases in a closed cylinder.

For the recent demonstration, the prototype device relied on an electric heating element. Future devices will instead rely on heat generated by the radioactive decay of strontium-90, a radioisotope that can be extracted from spent nuclear fuel .

Nuclear batteries have been in use for decades , primarily for space missions ranging from the Apollo moon shots to NASA’s Voyager spacecraft and Mars rovers . But the batteries being developed by Zeno Power promise to be at least four times more efficient than traditional radioisotope thermoelectric generators, Boles said.

Boles said the non-radiological test exceeded expectations. “There’s a difference between a design that works on paper and hardware that works in the field,” she said in a news release . “This is the moment our team has been building toward: proof that this technology works outside the lab.”

Long-lasting nuclear batteries could be used to power undersea sensor networks or recharge autonomous underwater vehicles. “There are a lot of applications, especially on the maritime front, that we really want electricity for,” Boles said. “And we really don’t need a ton of it. But we need it to be really reliable, and we need it to be long endurance, and we need it to be self-managed. … I think of it like a slow Tesla supercharger on the seabed.”
Retired Navy Adm. John Richardson, former chief of naval operations and a member of Zeno’s board of directors, called the recent test an “important step toward undersea superiority.”

“Protecting maritime infrastructure and powering distributed systems at sea requires energy; energy that lasts for years, not days or months,” Richardson said in a written statement. “As competition intensifies in contested domains, powered subsea systems will help keep us ahead. Zeno Power has steadily reduced risk, proven its technology, built a supply chain, and prepared to scale production.”

Next year, Zeno Power plans to install a radioisotope heat source in its generator and test the system in a water tank under controlled laboratory conditions. If those tests are successful, Zeno will move forward with the first operational seabed deployment of its radioisotope-fueled maritime system later in 2027.

The maritime battery isn’t Zeno’s only product. The company is also working on a nuclear-powered heater system for spacecraft, with a demonstration on the lunar surface planned as early as 2028 . Zeno’s broader vision is to provide long-lasting, reliable power on the moon and Mars, and in extreme environments on Earth.

Since its founding in 2018, Zeno has secured $105 million in private capital and has brought in $60 million in contracts with the Pentagon and NASA. The company has more than 95 employees at locations in Seattle, California and Washington, D.C., with the largest contingent working at its engineering headquarters in Seattle’s South Lake Union district .

articles.title: County Council Moves to Restore Weekend Vashon Water Taxi Service
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: An amendment approved this week by a King County Council budget committee is set to restore weekend fast ferry runs between Pier 50 in Downtown Seattle and Vashon Island after that service was sunsetted this fall. Via a half-penny increase to the county's Marine District property tax rate, seven round trips on Saturday and Sunday will be restored next year along with one additional Friday evening trip. In addition, the weekday mid-day trips currently on the schedule will be able to continue indefinitely.

The weekend runs had been enabled by a $1.1 million state earmark set aside in 2025 that ran out, an attempt by the legislature to supplement Washington State Ferries service. Prior to this spring when Sunday service got up-and-running, King County had not operated seven-day service on the Vashon water taxi since the 1990s. Without the water taxi in operation, anyone trying to get to Vashon Island has to utilize the state ferry terminals in West Seattle or Tacoma, which can add significant travel time for trips headed downtown.

Vashon Water taxi service has taken a big jump thanks to an expanded schedule. This September, the line provided 116% more rides than it did three years prior, with 30-40% of weekday riders now taking advantage of the added mid-day trips that hadn't previously existed. After seeing more than 155,000 riders in 2025, Vashon water taxi usage is on track to shatter that annual record, with more than 145,000 riders through the third quarter of 2026.

Put forward by Councilmember Teresa Mosqueda, this week's committee vote only received one vote in opposition, from South King County representative Steffanie Fain. Mosqueda, who represents the district that includes the fully unincorporated island, had been a champion for the water taxi at the legislature, working with State Senator Emily Alvarado (D-West Seattle, 34th Legislative District) on securing earmarks for the project in recent years.

"I want to thank the state legislature for the investments that they made in midday service and in weekend service. But we've heard very clearly from our state legislative partners, including the chair of the transportation committee in the Senate, that we should not expect there to be an ongoing source of revenue from the state legislature for water taxi service," Mosqueda told her colleagues.

Despite that clear shift away from providing funding for foot ferries at the legislature, many Vashon residents see King County fast ferry service as providing a critical fallback option when issues arise with Washington State Ferries service. Last month, when service on nearly every WSF route ground to a halt due to a crew shortage traced to a state employee labor dispute, the fast ferry was the only public option that Vashoners had to get on and off the island.

"Too many of our decision-makers see the water taxi as an optional nice-to-have service. But we all lived through the Oct. 5 ferry sick-out. The ferry shutdown made it plain that Vashon Island lives at the end of a fragile lifeline. We don’t have a bridge. We have the state ferries and the King County Metro water taxi," Amy Drayer, Rick Wallace and Wendy Aman, members of the Islanders for Ferry Action steering committee, wrote in the Vashon-Maury Island Beachcomber last month. "Decision-makers need to know that we need more water transportation, not less."

King County is one of the few jurisdictions across the state allowed to operate a passenger ferry district, along with Kitsap Transit, thanks to a special carve-out in state law. The Mosquito Fleet Act, put forward by Rep. Greg Nance (D-23rd, Bainbridge), was intended to expand that pool by letting more cities, counties, and port districts in on the ability to use local funding tools, but it has run into headwinds at the legislature over the past two legislative sessions.

Marko Liias (D-Edmonds, 21st LD) has been the most outspoken skeptic of the Mosquito Fleet Act in the state Senate, but its chances may improve in the future. Liias, who has served in the legislature since 2008, recently announced a run for Snohomish County Executive.

"I do think it's important to make sure that our all of our county residents have have connectivity and and transit, especially so they can rely on systems that will not necessarily need a car," Councilmember Jorge Barón said. "And so I see this as part of the infrastructure, though it's not directly in my district, but I think my district residents will maybe use the water taxi to go on the weekends as well."

Earlier this year, King County secured a $22.1 million federal grant to expand the Downtown fast ferry terminal at Pier 50, with Metro's General Manager Michelle Allison noting that the agency will be able to double the capacity of the existing terminal with that funding. Space had been tight at the downtown terminal with expansion of Kitsap Transit's fast ferry service to Bremerton and Kingston, but those runs also relied on state funding that has now run out .

Councilmembers were persuaded to fund extra service to Vashon thanks in part to the ridership numbers that King County has been clocking. Under its Marine District authority, the county is able to levy a property tax of 7.5 cents on every $100,000 of taxable value, but currently only utilizes 0.8 cents. With Mosqueda's amendment, that will go up to 1.3 cents.

"This wasn't a high priority for me in terms of this particular budget, but I did ask your office for the ridership numbers, [and] I heard from one of your constituents by email asking that this service be continued, and so I did a little bit more digging into it and what it would cost, and it is remarkably affordable," Council Budget Chair Rod Dembowski said to Mosqueda during this week's meeting. "I don't think lives stop midday, and they don't stop on the weekend."
The Marine District tax increase is set to be included in the county's mid-biennial budget update, set to be voted on November 24.

articles.title: County Council Advances RapidRide R Plan to Consolidate Route 7 Stops
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Plans to bring RapidRide to the Rainier Valley took a step forward Tuesday with a King County committee vote to approve the planned alignment and stop locations for the future R Line between Rainier Beach and Downtown Seattle. A major priority for King County Executive Girmay Zahilay, the overhaul of the existing Route 7 has drawn concerns around transit access, with a number of existing bus stops used by riders set to be consolidated together when the RapidRide line is built.

Slated to open by 2032, the $91.2 million RapidRide line along Rainier Avenue is set to come with infrastructure upgrades at stops, along with some speed and reliability upgrades on top of bus lanes that have already been added by the City of Seattle in recent years.

The 7 is already one of the most frequent buses in the system, which contributes to it being the second-busiest route Metro runs. As such, significant improvements in bus frequency aren't likely, but more trips may be added on nights and weekends.

Zahilay's administration is eyeing ways to accelerate rollout of the R Line, proposing a 2027 budget that would advance nearly two-thirds of the funding for the project in the hopes of showing a firmer commitment to the Seattle Department of Transportation, which is planning related upgrades along Rainier in future years.

While stop consolidation has traditionally been part of the RapidRide package elsewhere, Metro's plans to eliminate high-use stops like S Cloverdale Street and S Charles Street have proven unpopular among existing 7 riders. In addition, the R Line would modify the 7's route to directly serve Rainier Beach Station, eliminating service south of S Henderson Street including on the S Prentice Street loop where some 7 trips currently terminate.

The R Line has been on the books for over a decade, envisioned as one of a slate of transit corridors to be funded by the 2015 Seattle Transportation Levy. But the project was put on hold in 2021 in the wake of pandemic-related budget cuts.

When Metro restarted outreach on the project earlier this summer, the plans for stop consolidation – controversial even at the time – were largely the same, though a pair of stops around Mount Baker did get re-added ahead of transmittal to the County Council in response to feedback this fall .

King County Metro has downplayed the impact of that planned stop consolidation, noting that 12 out of 16 stops north of Henderson Street set to be eliminated are currently served by other buses – even if those buses go in very different directions, like the crosstown Route 50. However, the ordinance adopted Tuesday does not actually set future stop locations for the R Line in stone, instead requiring the county council to be notified if there are any changes to the plan.

Councilmember Rhonda Lewis, who was Zahilay's top aide before winning appointment to the District 2 seat that he represented until being elected County Executive last year, praised the R Line in comments ahead of Tuesday's vote, while at the same time noting the potential impacts that could come from having fewer bus stops on Rainier.

"For older riders and riders with disabilities, the walk to the next stop is no small thing. Many neighbors have also told me that they feel safer waiting at Cloverdale than at the stops nearby," Lewis said. "Today's vote settles the route and its stations. However, I'm grateful to hear that Metro has committed to keep the conversation with constituents going through design and construction to ensure community concerns are heard. My constituents in District 2 have waited a long time for this line, and I am proud to see it move forward today."
Lewis's colleague Claudia Balducci struck a much more concerned tone.

"When we hear from members of the surrounding community as plaintively as we have heard from this community that this service will actually be a degradation because of loss of stops," Balducci said. "Frequent and reliable service is only as good as people's ability to get on it, and I'm very concerned that I'm hearing, this kicking of the can down the road: 'Yes, we'll keep talking to the community.' But we are today, and at the council meeting [next week], we'll be taking a vote to reduce access to transit in this corridor."

Committee chair Steffanie Fain afforded Zahilay's administration and King County Metro more deference than Balducci. Fain represents South King County, where Metro is currently building the RapidRide I line – a project that has had its own twists and turns when it comes to getting to construction.

"I did appreciate that Metro added back two stops based on that feedback, and so I think that the RapidRide R line won't work without community partnerships, and that they are building those and are responding to those," Fain said. "And I think the community appreciates that. If I could be so bold as to say that I know that this is ongoing work and, nothing's perfect, but certainly I appreciate the collaboration with the community."

Balducci also raised issues with accelerating the funding for the R Line without a clear picture of what exactly that funding will achieve in 2027, while the project is still in planning. Metro is currently facing an uncertain financial future, with the agency's fiscal reserves set to start to run out by the early 2030s, but decisions around how to deal with that reality aren't expected to be put forward until next year's budget cycle.

"We are holding that money unspent intentionally in 2027, apparently because our friends at SDOT need to see that there's money sitting in a box in order to feel comfortable moving forward," Balducci said. "That is not a resounding statement of support for this project by our colleagues in SDOT. And also, what a waste to put aside tens of millions of dollars for no purpose."

Transit advocates are still waiting to see a full analysis of the time savings that will come from the full R Line package, which as presented earlier this year will leave out transit priority treatments along one of the 7's most problematic stretches – along S Jackson Street through the International District.

"That's what I'd love to see because I think then we could have a better conversation about okay, maybe there's places where it really makes sense to eliminate stops, but if you're just making people's walks longer and you're not actually making the commute time significantly shorter or the travel time..." Anna Zivarts, founder of the Nondrivers Alliance, told The Urbanist last month on a bus tour of Rainier Avenue.

Zivarts has been pushing to broaden the conversation about what the R Line can do to improve transit access, potentially even looking at different transit corridors that aren't available today, including all-day connections directly to Capitol Hill and First Hill.

"There's a lot of folks using the bus to travel locally within Rainier Valley, and commuting to downtown as efficiently as possible is not necessarily the top priority for a lot of folks who are using transit right now on this road," Zivarts said. "So we need to make sure we're meeting those needs with whatever investment [we make]. We'd love more investments in transit, yes, but let's make sure we're serving the people who are relying on it currently in this area."

Lewis did not participate in Tuesday's committee vote, which was unanimous. In fact, the county's transportation committee includes no members who represent Seattle, in what is likely a first in King County history. Next week, former state Senator Rebecca Saldaña will take office as Zahilay's permanent replacement to represent District 2, likely just a few hours after this ordinance gets a full council vote.
Though the R Line is moving forward, the conversation around its exact design is certain to continue.

articles.title: Democrats Secure Supermajority in State House, but Fall Short in Senate
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: Just about everything that could break Democrats' way in 2026 Washington State House races did, but the state Senate was a different story. Senate Democrats failed to make gains after Carolina Mejia's three-point election night lead evaporated in later returns in the Legislative District 35 race.
As a result, they'll have no pickups in the Senate, but stay at a comfortable 30-19 edge. That's still three seats short of a 2/3 supermajority.

Thanks to 10 seats they have tentatively flipped from Republicans, Democrats' advantage in the state House will grow from 59-39 to 69-29. That works out to70% of seats, surpassing the 2/3 supermajority threshold, which makes overriding a governor's veto or passing a state constitutional amendment possible without Republican votes.

Jenn Marie Strickling was the last Democrat to surpass her challenger, passing incumbent Rep. Cyndy Jacobsen in the second week of counting. As of November 17, Strickling was leading by 80 votes, with very few votes remaining to count. Pierce County estimates just 10 remaining ballots to count countywide, as of Tuesday.

"We feel extremely confident these results will hold," Strickling told The Urbanist Tuesday. "The blue wave this year reached all the way into the 25th, but what we're seeing here is also the result of a grassroots effort that's been years in the making. It’s the product of neighbors coming together, building relationships, and refusing to give up on their community."
If the lead stays near 0.14 percentage points (below the one quarter of one percent threshold), this would be headed to a manual recount, which is unlikely to change the outcome.

Why Democrats were able to win 10 seats in the state House while gaining none in the Senate was a bit of a fluke regarding which seats were up for election this year. Since state senators get four-year terms, only half of the districts are up in each even-year election.

Democrats' biggest gains were achieved in Legislative District 14, 17, 18, and 25, where they flipped two House seats (barring Strickling's narrow lead reversing). In each of those districts no Senate seats were up, but they will be in 2028.

Vancouver Democrat Adrian Cortes already flipped the LD18 seat in 2024, which was an early sign that Clark County's political alignment was shifting. On the other hand, LD14, LD17, and LD25 Senate seats are held by Republicans and will be key pickup opportunities. The 2028 election will allow Democrats a chance to flip seats on the Senate side, and Republicans certainly will be pressed to hold them, given the steady erosion of their stronghold political territory.

Willoughby's win also demonstrated that Democrats can win in LD12, providing another pickup opportunity. While the national mood played a big role, Democrats also smartly tailored attacks to their specific opponent in LD12, emphasizing Rep. Brian Burnett's personal ties to right-wing extremism. Opponents highlighted lawsuits against the sheriff’s office Burnett previously led, as well as his ties to the ultra-conservative Grace City Church, which has aligned itself with Christian nationalism.
Traditional Republican strongholds like LD35 and LD39 also saw much closer races even as Republicans held on, suggesting they could be in play in another blue wave year, if that momentum continues.

In shifting legislative districts, voters who were worried about the rising cost of housing, transportation, and other necessities appeared to give Democrats the edge. In addition to pointing to affordability, the incoming crop of candidates gave credit to campaigning hard, listening earnestly to voters, and pledging to boldly pursue solutions.

"I believe a significant part of our success came from showing up and having genuine conversations with people. We spent months knocking on doors, listening to concerns, and discussing the issues affecting families across the district," Christly told The Urbanist . "What I consistently heard was frustration over the rising cost of living, housing affordability, access to healthcare, and the challenges facing our schools and small businesses. Those concerns crossed political lines."
Campaigning hard, hitting the doors, and running as a united slate appeared part of the recipe for success in LD25, too.

"This was a multi-year effort," Strickling said. "Together with my stellar running mate David Berg, our team made more than 26,000 door attempts and over 50,000 phone calls. Most of our support came from everyday people in a community that was hungry for change. Dark money PACs came after us, and we won anyway. At the doors we talked about rent, wages, schools and whether people's kids can afford to stay here. We built this infrastructure from the ground up, with grassroots support and community relationships that will be durable long into the future."
Like Christly, Strickling and Berg pointed to this restlessness in the electorate and desire for change.

"For me, this is personal," Strickling said. "I grew up in Orting. I've worked construction as a LiUNA laborer, built successful businesses, and organized with neighbors who were told nobody in power would listen. Folks here want a paycheck that covers the bills, a home they can afford to stay in, and a government that answers to them. That's what they voted for, and that's what I intend to fight for."
Alongside living wages, Strickling pointed to housing as central to this fight.

"Keeping people in their homes comes first," Strickling said. "On the Pierce County Charter Review Commission I fought for protections for manufactured homeowners, many of them seniors and working families who did everything right and still faced losing homes they'd paid for. I'm taking that fight to Olympia for every homeowner and tenant in this district."

"I'm excited to bring a new kind of representation to the 25th LD," Berg told The Urbanist . "Voters want to be heard and want to be a part of finding solutions to the issues we're all facing. During the campaign I regularly heard from people who had never seen their legislators. Hearing their stories and continuing to engage with them will help me make better policies in Olympia."
As a school board director, Berg said education would be a focus. Many successful candidates ran on fully funding schools and improving educational outcomes.

"I've been a long time advocate for public education and I'm looking forward to continuing that work. Voters also told me they are concerned about digital privacy and AI, and the Legislature has an important role to play in addressing those concerns," Berg said. "I also heard repeatedly about affordability issues and utility costs. We can do more to help bring down rising costs and I'm excited to be a part of finding solutions for our families."
Likewise, the newly minted LD17 representative pointed to a determination to tackle affordability and strengthen the educational and health care systems.

"Affordability will be at the center of my work, particularly housing, healthcare, and the everyday costs affecting working families," Christly said. "I also want to focus on strengthening public education, supporting small businesses, expanding access to healthcare in our rural communities, and investing responsibly in infrastructure."
Like Berg, Christly pointed to a desire to transcend partisanship and work together across partisan lines.

"First and foremost, I'm incredibly grateful for the trust voters have placed in me," Christly told The Urbanist . "This election represents an opportunity to bring a different perspective to Olympia, one grounded in listening, practical problem-solving, and a willingness to work with people regardless of political affiliation. The 17th District is diverse, encompassing growing suburban communities, small towns, and rural areas, each with its own challenges. My responsibility now is to represent all of those communities, including the people who didn't vote for me."

Democrats have a real shot at a supermajority. They have seats to spare in the state House, and four seats that they could flip in the Senate. If they hold their current seats and flip three, they will have a Senate supermajority to go with the House one.

A supermajority would be a huge chance to fundamentally shift state policy and institutions. For example, lawmakers could erase the highly dubious 1932 precedent the state Supreme Court set barring the progressive taxation of income, overruling state voters who had just passed an income tax. Other possibilities include enshrining reproductive rights or climate action in the state constitution, or paving the way for a land value tax .

Short of a constitutional amendment, the ability to override a governor's veto could also give the Democratic caucus more leverage in negotiations with Governor Bob Ferguson, who has often used the threat of a veto to strongarm them and take more progressive policy ideas off the table.

While Ferguson's term is up in 2028, last month he reminded a room full of corporate leaders – some of whom has raised millions to begin running negative ads against the governor – that he plans on being governor for a long time. After Democrats ran the tables in the November election, Ferguson and the state's corporate elite quickly buried the hatchet, with the governor ordering a freeze on corporate regulations .
Strickling took a harder line than the governor in her comments to The Urbanist: "I want to put Big Tech in check so the biggest companies play by the same rules as our small businesses."

Big business campaign spending in the state largely failed to bear fruit. Five of six races the Microsoft-backed Washington Needs to Compete political action committee (PAC) invested more than $1.7 million collectively went toward the more progressive candidate, rather than the conservative candidates the PAC was backing.

Three races where Urbanist-endorsed progressive challengers targeted conservative-leaning Democrat incumbents saw flips: Jessica Forsythe (LD48-2), Krista Perez (LD29-1), and Kelabe Tewolde (LD37-2). Forsythe prevailed even with conservative PACs spending more than a million dollars to attack her and prop up incumbent Rep. Amy Walen, one of only a handful of Democrats to oppose the millionaires tax.
In open seat races, progressives also made some inroads.

In LD29, Urbanist-endorsed Patrick Stickney prevailed in a close race with Tacoma Councilmember Joe Bushnell. These intra-party wins for progressives will shift the caucus to the left, with incumbent progressives also generally defending their seats, too, despite the corporate money thrown at dislodging them.
In LD32, Urbanist-endorsed candidate Danica Noble held off centrist Keith Scully, winning by three points.
In LD23, conservative megadonors threw a ton of money at unseating Urbanist-endorsed progressive incumbent Rep. Tarra Simmons (LD23-1), but came up short.

The 2026 election results are a heartening sign that strong campaigns can overcome copious political spending from elite megadonors. On the other hand, frequently running an uphill race is not a great position to be in.
For now, Democrats can enjoy their largest House majority in modern history. The 2027 session convenes on January 11, and Democrats will put their expanded caucus to work.

articles.title: History of automated train control
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: As I explained a few years ago , automating new lines and even existing lines would have many advantages. Even Sound Transit has recently considered automating the Ballard extension. Some people still consider automated train control (ATC) as unproven even though many airports (SeaTac, JFK AirTrain…) and subways use this technology such as Vancouver Skytrain and new lines on Hawaii and in Montreal already use the technology. Let’s look at the history .

Automating trains is much easier than having fully autonomous cars. As long as the trains run on tracks in a separate right of way, no complex video or even lidar systems are required but track sensors and a more powerful signaling and train control system. Platform doors are often added for additional safety.

Boston already started to experiment with automating trains in 1901. Berlin in 1928. Paris operated a short line from 1952 to 1957 but didn’t have funds for upgrades until the first main line was upgraded in 1966. More lines have been upgraded since. Tokyo started limited operation in 1962, more lines have been added since. Hitachi automated the Disney and Linimo monorail. London started tests in 1968. The Victoria Underground Line finally started fully automated operations in 1967.
While initially the trains still had a driver, fully driverless operation started in Kobe (Japan) and later in Lille (France), Barcelona and airports such as JFK.
In Nürnberg (Germany) they even allowed mixed operation between traditional and driverless trains in 2008.

More modern light metros such as Vancouver’s Skytrain (in 1985), London’s Dockland Light Railway (in 1987) and Copenhagen were designed as automated systems from the beginning allowing for shorter trains without a cab, smaller stations, and higher frequency. Recent new lines in Montreal (REM) and Hawaii also leveraged these advantages. Now many systems around the world are driverless. While Italian Ansaldo/Hitachi Rail STS developed their train systems around ATC, established rail provides ( Alstom Urbalis Fluence and Siemens Trainguard MT ) added ATC support to some of their existing rail offerings. Siemens AutomatedTrain effort is even automating regular heavy rail operation including the video detection of obstacles along the tracks.

As I explained in my prior post, Sound Transit had evaluated various modes in 2014. This included automated light metro systems such as Skytrain. At that time they decided on light rail technology for the spine to allow for both DSTT as well as at-grade operation. However, for some extensions Sound Transit is now planning, such as Ballard, it might be better to keep them separate rather than interlining them to leverage ATC advantages such as higher frequency and smaller stations.

As the northern Link line is fully grade separated, Link trains could even run fully automated from Everett to downtown. This would allow more precise acceleration and breaking, reduced headways (as close as 60sec) and faster turnaround at the end of the line, reducing the need for pocket tracks. Alstrom claims it reduces trackside equipment usage by up to 20% and energy consumption by up to 30%.
I hope Sound Transit would seriously consider automation where feasible.

articles.title: ‘Do you want love? Do you want tea?’ — Persian cafe by day, disco by night in Open Form’s first year on Capitol Hill
articles.author: CHS
paras: Open Form has been brewing tea, pouring wine, and spinning records out of its dreamy, second-level loft overlooking E Pike. Over its first year, the space has carved out its own niche in Capitol Hill’s cafe scene, evolving into more than just a coffee shop.

The concept began in 2025 when Tara Almassi returned to her hometown of Seattle after 12 years in New York City, unsure of her next steps in life. In New York, Almassi had been the one to host elaborate dinner parties for her girlfriends in her Brooklyn apartment. Drawing on a background in production and fashion, she wanted to find new ways to curate a gathering space that would inspire community and connection.
“I wanted to move back and create a space that I would want to hang out in,” Almassi said. She often refers to Open Form as “my house”.

On a lucky day, the loft’s oversized windows flood the room with sunlight, while long communal tables and couches invite guests to share the space with their neighbors, prompting conversation as the whirls of the espresso machine and soft pop music fade into the background.
“I think Seattle needs more of this kind of space; a space for people to want to explore different parts of themselves,” she said.
That instinct for hospitality runs deep. Born and raised in Seattle, Almassi said her parents were Iranian immigrants and passed down the “natural art of hosting.”
“That is really the root of me,” Almassi said. “The core of being Iranian is that they love bringing people together and building community.”

Before every family *mehmooni,* which Almassi describes as a Persian gathering, dinner, or party, she would watch her mother light candles around the house and lay out more than enough food and drinks for everyone, always in awe of how intentional her mother became regarding the smallest details.

“Our parents, they would have dinner and have a couple glasses of wine. And then all of a sudden, the music would turn on and they would all move the furniture and start dancing,” Almassi said, remembering the abundance of love and joy she felt at those gatherings. “[Iranian people] are truly the most kind-hearted, warm, inviting people. They just pick people – even if they didn’t know them – they would grab their hand, pull them in to dance.”

Almassi never wanted Open Form to be locked into “being one thing,” and over its first year since opening in October 2025 , the loft has taken shape as a cafe, wine shop, nighttime venue, and open workspace. Still, she was surprised by just how much their nightlife events took off.

After the sun dips out of view and DJs start taking records out of their sleeves and the room turns atmospheric, a shift Almassi describes as feeling like “you’re entering someone’s home for a dance party.”

“People dance here, and I love that, but it wasn’t in the cards,” Almassi said of the DJ sets and jazz nights, where dancing with friends and strangers became an expression of spontaneity and whimsy echoing the *mehmoonis* of her childhood. “I saw how much this space makes people come out of their shell and just want to have a good time. And they feel safe, which I feel so lucky to have created that.”

A standout from that first year has been Skin Contact , Open Form’s most popular residency, which brings disco to the space every second Thursday of the month. Regularly booked artists like Théque Support and Supreme La Rock have helped the team build out their “vinyl-focused” sound system, anchored by celebrations like their Studio 54-inspired Halloween night.
By day, the menu reflects Almassi’s personal approach to hospitality, pairing coffee and matcha with craft beer, an Iranian-inspired tea service, and a curated wine list.

Having fallen in love with wine tasting in New York, Almassi views wine as a form of storytelling. Her collection, which she plans to spotlight further with dedicated monthly wine nights in year two, features primarily natural, biodynamic bottles from French and Middle Eastern winemakers. She built the list through “real world experience” and trial and error.
“I don’t want to come at it from a pretentious angle,” Almassi said. “It’s truly just: these are all things that I just love myself and I hope that everyone else will love it too.”
Or how about a dish of ice cream (Image: Open Form)

Tea carries an equally personal weight. Looking ahead to expanding the menu — potentially with a custom “tea bar” — Almassi reflects on the afternoons she spent sipping warm tea at the dining room table with her grandmother. For many Persian families, tea is a daily ritual to slow down and be present, acting as a love language of its own.

“Tea is such a grounding part of us [Iranian people] and how we communicate and show our love for each other,” Almassi said. “Whenever somebody comes over, it’s like, ‘Do you want love? Do you want tea?’”

Whether it’s an unfamiliar ingredient in an Iranian tea, a natural wine, or an artist spinning on a weeknight, Open Form spent its first year creating an environment that begs questions—and encourages guests to be curious about the people sitting nearby.

“It’s so important to be around people and to get to know people and to be curious,” Almassi said. “That was a big part of what I wanted to bring in here … just that warmth and intentionality and this idea of everyone feeling cared for.”
Find Open Form at 500 E Pike. Learn more at openform.space .

articles.title: Capitol Hill SOS? Roma Roma says it needs more business to survive, regulars rallying to help Chandelier Lounge after costly vandalism
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Two neighborhood venues are hoping customers will show up to help them through some rough patches doing business on Capitol Hill. 12th Ave’s Roma Roma is taking the unusual step of announcing that business is so slow it might have to close. On Broadway, customers are rallying to help out Chandelier Lounge after costly vandalism.

At Roma Roma, chef Forrest Brunton is sounding the alarm. In a candid video update shared with the community, Brunton said that strong customer praise has not translated into the revenue required to keep the business afloat.

“It’s been a hard year for Seattle restaurants and we’re no exception, we might have to close,” Brunton said in the announcement posted last week. Reflecting on his decades in the industry and his debut as a restaurant owner, Brunton described the disconnect between customer reception and financial survival. “In my time here, I’ve never worked at a place that got such positive feedback but still struggled so much to do the business we need to survive.”

CHS reported here as Brunton and his brother opened Roma Roma in February with Roman-style pizza sold by the pound in the space formerly home to the Capitol Hill Racher’s Ginger Beer . The by-the-pound element has reportedly been cut as the brothers have tried to streamline the experience and let their excellent pizza shine.
Despite the uncertain outlook, Brunton said the team loves their regulars and the neighborhood, encouraging locals to visit the restaurant “while you still can” and share feedback or suggestions.
Roma Roma plans to lean into creative menu offerings and community events. “We’re not laying down and dying, we’re going to double down on the stuff we really love,” Brunton said.
On Broadway, regulars are taking things into their own hands to help the Chandelier Lounge.
Last week, the 2024-born lounge and Thai joint was hit by costly property damage. This Friday, they are planning a support event at Chandelier.
“This amazing local venue deserves better. Let’s pack this place this week and show them how much they are loved,” the event invite reads.
Roma Roma is located at 1610 12th Ave. Learn more at romaroma.pizza .

articles.title: Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence to hold Trans Day of Remembrance Vigil on Capitol Hill
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: The Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, Abbey of St. Joan , will host a Trans Day of Remembrance Vigil on Friday on Capitol Hill.
The gathering invites community members to share grief, receive a blessing, and honor transgender and gender-expansive people lost to gender-based violence.

This year’s vigil after state voters approved Initiative 638 barring transgender girls from competing on K–12 female school sports teams and mandating biological sex verification, a measure currently facing legal challenges from civil rights groups and Seattle Public Schools ahead of its December 3rd effective date.

Advocates say that heightened political scrutiny often coincides with persistent threats to safety. According to tracking by the Human Rights Campaign Foundation and Advocates for Trans Equality , at least 399 transgender and gender non-conforming people were killed in the United States between 2013 and late 2025, with 27 violent deaths documented in the 2025 reporting year. Black transgender women bear a disproportionate burden, accounting for 63% of those recorded killings in 2025, underscoring the call for solidarity at Friday’s memorial.

Trans Day of Remembrance Vigil Friday, November 20, 2026 3:00pm-4:00pm ​ Peer Seattle, 1520 Bellevue Ave Ste 100 ​ Join the Sisters of Perpetual Indulgence, Abbey of St. Joan, for a vigil honoring those who have lost their lives to gender-based violence. The gathering will include a vigil, a blessing from the Sisters, and time to come together, share, grieve, and support one another.

articles.title: Last chance for public comment before Seattle City Council votes on 2027–2028 budget
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: You have one final opportunity to have your say before the Seattle City Council votes to adopt the 2027–2028 budget at a special meeting on Friday at 1:00 PM. Following Thursday’s Select Budget Committee session where only written testimony is permitted, Friday’s full Council meeting at City Hall at 600 4th Ave opens with up to one hour of live public comment, limited to two minutes per speaker.

In-person speakers must sign up inside Council Chambers by 12:45 PM, while remote sign-ups open online at noon. Written comments sent to Council@seattle.gov before 10:00 AM Friday will be distributed prior to the vote.

The final vote caps a contentious week in which council members approved more than 100 amendments to Mayor Katie Wilson’s spending plan, which had originally been shaped to close a projected $175 million shortfall without dipping into reserves or new taxes.

The council had other ideas. To fund its priorities, the council’s balancing package relies on major revenue shifts and compromises including raiding the JumpStart payroll tax originally intended to fund affordable housing and services:

Wilson warned this week that relying on roughly $31 million in one-time funds for ongoing programs risks creating a $58 million deficit in 2028 and beyond. Friday, we’ll hear what people have to say about that as the council makes its final vote on the budget.

articles.title: The Station's Columbia City Coffee Shop Closes Its Doors
paras: The Station in Columbia City, a popular coffee shop and community gathering space, closed its doors in mid-November. The interior of the shop is nearly empty, and red eviction notices are taped to the locked glass doors.

The notices said anyone who remained in the building after 11:59 p.m. on Nov. 16 would be evicted by officers from the King County Sheriff's Office. In the days before the deadline, people were seen loading equipment, tables, and other items from the shop into a truck.

The reason for the Columbia City shop's closure is unknown. On Nov. 17, the shop posted a public statement on an Instagram reel with video showing the space emptied of furniture and equipment. "When we first started, people told us not to open a business in the area because of all the heavy, dark history," the statement read. "Despite those warnings we took the leap, and we are so very thankful to Columbia City for welcoming us so warmly for almost 3 years!"
When the Emerald contacted Station co-owner Jose Luis Rodriguez about the closure, Rodriguez texted that he had no comment.
A representative with the King County Sheriff's Office said they could not disclose any information about the eviction notice.

On Nov. 18, an employee closing up the Beacon Hill shop spoke about the Columbia City location. "Business wasn't good in the area," said the employee, who didn't provide a name. "It's a difficult time for small businesses."

In December 2025, the Emerald reported on allegations of harassment and unwanted touching against Rodriguez. In interviews at the time, he acknowledged making vulgar remarks and denied touching his grandniece, one of the women who came forward. No criminal charges have been filed against Rodriguez in connection with the allegations.
In the Instagram post, The Station expressed gratitude toward its Columbia City patrons. "Thank you for being such an incredible community and for supporting us along the way."

articles.title: The unthinkable has come to pass: Tom Brady is a pretty good broadcaster
articles.author: Alex Kirshner
paras: The former NFL quarterback was widely derided when he started his job in the Fox booth. But he has shown a human side and explains the game beautifully

I have accidentally force-fed myself Tom Brady’s commentary as my primary means of watching the NFL this season. When my favorite team, the Steelers, hired Mike McCarthy as head coach , I lodged a silent protest by declining to spend the several hundred dollars needed to get NFL Sunday Ticket. I didn’t even splurge for RedZone. That means I’ve found myself watching Fox’s NFL broadcasts on a Sunday – often an underwhelming Cowboys game – where Brady is the color commentator in the network’s No 1 booth, alongside play-by-play man Kevin Burkhardt.

This two-and-a-half-month experiment has led me to an alarming conclusion, one I’d seen others reaching gradually over the last year but never taken too seriously myself. Recently, though, the truth has become unavoidable: Tom Brady is pretty good at his job. Gone are the days of the best quarterback of all time being hopelessly outmatched on TV. What has changed is that Brady now sounds like an actual human being.

articles.title: A doctor’s guide to surviving — and enjoying — holiday feasting while on GLP-1 medication
articles.author:
<name>Reed Berger-Fleishman, Associate Clinical Professor of Medicine and Surgery, University of Illinois Chicago</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/reed-berger-fleishman-2764205"/>
paras: Thanksgiving and the winter holidays bring celebration, connection and plenty of opportunities to come together with family and friends.

But the holiday season also brings something else: more food-centered gatherings, larger portions and richer foods than most people typically eat throughout the year. Think whipped sweet potatoes, mac and cheese, decadent side dishes and an abundance of desserts.

For people taking GLP-1 medications for diabetes management, weight loss or other medical reasons, these celebrations can present unique challenges. Changes in appetite, smaller portion tolerance, limits on alcohol consumption, medication side effects and the desire to maintain progress can make navigating holiday traditions feel a little different.

As a physician specializing in obesity medicine , I encourage my patients to view GLP-1 medications as an advantage during the holidays. These medications can help regulate appetite, improve awareness of fullness, and reinforce healthier eating behaviors during a season when food often takes center stage.

However, these medications don’t eliminate the possibility of overindulgence. In fact, patients who previously experienced little or no nausea due to GLP-1s may suddenly develop significant nausea or even vomiting after eating beyond their new comfort level. Nothing can derail a holiday celebration quite like an upset stomach. Accounting for how these medications affect your body can help you avoid uncomfortable surprises while still enjoying the foods and traditions you love.

Whether taken by injection or orally, GLP-1 medications have become increasingly popular worldwide for managing Type 2 diabetes , obesity and other chronic conditions. In the United States, approximately 1 in 10 adults used these drugs in 2025, and prescribing rates continue to climb.

GLP-1 medications work by reducing hunger, slowing stomach emptying and helping patients feel full sooner and stay full longer . Many patients also report fewer cravings for high-calorie foods and even a reduced desire to drink alcohol .

In many ways, these effects can make holiday food temptations easier to navigate. My patients often tell me that they already know which dietary changes they need to make, but GLP-1 medications help them put those changes into practice. They find it easier to stop eating when they’re satisfied, resist unnecessary snacking and avoid the constant thoughts about food that previously made weight management so challenging.

One of the most important things you can do during the holidays is to learn to recognize your body’s changing fullness signals . Pay attention to nausea, bloating and early fullness rather than pushing yourself to finish everything on your plate.

These symptoms can serve as reminders that you’ve reached your comfortable limit. The best plan is to enjoy smaller portions, eat slowly and pause between bites to give your body time to recognize fullness. Rich, high-fat foods in particular can worsen nausea and prolong the sensation of fullness. A few bites of your favorite dishes may be much more satisfying than an entire serving.
GLP-1 medications don’t make these decisions for you – but they can reinforce healthier behaviors.

Alcohol deserves special consideration during the holidays, when social gatherings and celebrations often revolve around drinking . Although you may have tolerated alcohol without difficulty in the past, GLP-1 medications can change your experience.
Some patients report that GLP-1 medications reduce their desire for alcohol altogether. For them, the holidays may represent their first opportunity to drink since starting treatment.

Alcohol can worsen nausea, acid reflux, dehydration and other gastrointestinal symptoms that some patients already experience while taking GLP-1 medications. If you choose to drink, consider these precautions:
Limit your intake. Start with less than you might have consumed before starting your medication.
Avoid drinking on an empty stomach. Eat beforehand, but avoid a particularly large or high-fat meal.
Stay hydrated. Drink water throughout the occasion.
Pay attention to how you feel. Stop drinking if you experience nausea, dizziness or other unpleasant symptoms.
The safest approach is to be cautious and recognize that alcohol can aggravate medication-related gastrointestinal symptoms.
Holiday travel can disrupt established routines, medication schedules and access to prescriptions. A little planning can help prevent unnecessary interruptions in treatment.

Plan ahead for medication storage. Some injectable GLP-1 medications require refrigeration before use, while others allow room-temperature storage for a specified period after dispensing or first use. Storage requirements vary considerably by product. Check the prescribing information for your specific medication or ask your pharmacist before traveling. Don’t assume that all injectable medications can remain unrefrigerated for the same length of time.

If you’re flying, keep your medication and supplies in your carry-on luggage. This helps protect them from extreme temperatures and prevents problems if your checked luggage gets delayed or lost. Keep in mind that you might also need to have a note from your prescribing provider to carry them on.

Arrange prescription refills in advance. If you anticipate needing a refill while traveling, contact your pharmacy and prescribing clinician ahead of time. Prescribing and dispensing regulations can complicate obtaining medications in another state, so don’t wait until you run out.

Stick to your regular dosing schedule. Don’t take an extra dose or double up on medication to accommodate a holiday meal or try to suppress your appetite further. Taking more medication than prescribed can increase the risk of significant side effects and potentially cause an overdose . If travel disrupts your dosing schedule or you miss a dose, follow the instructions for your specific medication, or contact your prescribing clinician or pharmacist.
When in doubt, plan ahead and ask for guidance rather than making medication adjustments on your own.
Perhaps the most important advice I give my patients is this: The holidays are not everyday life, and one large meal or dessert will not erase the progress you’ve made.

You don’t need to skip Thanksgiving dinner, avoid your favorite dessert or feel guilty about enjoying a special meal. Maintaining a healthy relationship with food means allowing yourself flexibility while keeping your long-term goals in perspective.

At the same time, don’t let one celebratory meal turn into several weeks of abandoning the habits that have helped you succeed. Enjoy the occasion, recognize when you’ve had enough, and return to your usual routine afterward.
