articles.title: Xi-Putin-Trump summit was heavy on symbolism, light on substance – and not exactly a Yalta II
articles.author:
<name>Rana Mitter, Professor of U.S.-Asia Relations, Harvard Kennedy School</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/rana-mitter-2514498"/>
paras: It was touted as a history-making summit of the year. Presidents Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping sat down on Nov. 19, 2026, in Shenzhen, China, on the sideline of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit , for the first such trilateral meeting of the three leaders.
Going into the talks, the trio had much to dicuss: the ongoing war in Ukraine , Middle East conflict and the march of artificial intelligence technology chief among them.
But what did 90 minutes of conversation deliver?
As an expert on U.S.-China relations at Harvard Kennedy School , I saw a lot of style, but less substance.

The first thing to pay attention to is the symbolism of the occasion. And so much of what was presented in Shenzhen was about the body language of the three men, their interactions and what that may indicate in regards to how they view themselves in a potentially new global order.

And this was on show even before the leaders sat down. At the beginning of the trip, when Trump landed in Shenzhen, he was met by Xi . Meeting a foreign leader at the airport is seen as a special honor bestowed by the Chinese president.
And then came a hug – that really was unprecedented. I haven’t seen the general secretary of the Chinese Communist Party hug anyone before – certainly not his Politburo comrades.

It was all choreographed, of course. But it continued into the summit itself. The picture of a big table with Trump, Putin and Xi there is also symbolic. And look who was in the middle: Xi. Here we have China presenting as the “Middle Kingdom ,” steadying the world. Whether that is an accurate depiction of China’s global presence is beside the point – it is how Xi would like Beijing to be seen.
In terms of policy, however, not much was actually done, but we did get a glimpse of what was on the three leaders’ minds.

So we had talk of reforming the U.N. – something all three agree needs to be done. In particular, China wants more power in the organization, while Trump has become increasingly disillusioned with the international body.

And there was also a lot of discussion on nuclear weapons controls . In fact, all three signed off on a document that made statements and aspirations – with fewer commitments – to tamping down nuclear threats. Interestingly, this was all based around a phrase that U.S. President Ronald Reagan and Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev first aired in 1985 : “Nuclear war cannot be won, must never be fought.”

All three leaders signed onto the phrase, although there was not an awful lot of substance on how nuclear controls would be implemented. The main treaties on the matter expired a while ago , and Beijing, which lags behind Washington and Moscow in regards to capacity, may have different thoughts on the matter.
The big thing not discussed in any substantive way was the wars raging in the domains of two of the three nations.

For Trump, that means Iran. Washington has not been able to bring the conflict in Iran to a conclusion some nine months after it began. The thinking going into the summit may have been that if China – or even Russia – were able to help pressure Iran and bring an end to the conflict, that would be encouraged.

But the spectacle of the U.S. not being able to end the war in Iran is not, I suspect, something that the Russians and Chinese are in a rush to bring to an end. In any case, neither appeared willing to give up a key card – assistance to Washington in the matter – in this meeting.

At the other end of that Eurasian spectrum is Ukraine. It was not mentioned by name at the summit. Besides the fact that the three leaders are not on the same side of the conflict, there is also the fact that Ukraine’s European allies were not in the room – and it would have been far too much for Europe for Trump to make news on Ukraine in the company of Putin and Xi.

Beyond those conflicts, AI regulation and critical mineral supply chains were not discussed by the three leaders. But that isn’t to say that those issues – crucial ones in the U.S.-China economic rivalry – were not brought up in the bilateral conversations that took place in Shenzhen. It may be that they were heard in these more discreet, private settings.

There were some immediate similarities with the Yalta Conference – the February 1945 summit at which the U.K.’s Winston Churchill, Joseph Stalin of the Soviet Union and U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt planned out the end of World War II and began discussing postwar Europe. But these were largely about the imagery of the three men around the table.
Of course, the big three then included Britain; there was no China. That alone tells you how much geopolitics has changed over 80 years.
Also, Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill were all on the same side in 1945. It was a case of comrades in arms that would soon be drifting apart as the Cold War developed.
Here it may well be the other way around. China and Russia are partners, but the U.S. is seen as their adversary.

What Trump may want is detente rather than a new Cold War. Does this mean an emerging policy of Russia, China and the U.S. coming together in a new order? I imagine the Europeans may have something to say about that.

articles.title: Myanmar genocide ruling is a watershed moment in international justice – with huge ramifications for other cases
articles.author:
<name>Max Pensky, Co-Director, Institute for Genocide and Mass Atrocity Prevention, Binghamton University, State University of New York</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/max-pensky-392826"/>
paras: The International Court of Justice’s historic ruling of genocide against Myanmar on Nov. 19, 2026, will have significant consequences for the parties involved in the case – and potentially some who are not.

The Hague’s highly anticipated judgment in Gambia v. Myanmar is a major victory for Gambia, the tiny west African nation that filed a complaint with the court against Myanmar in 2019. It is also a major moment of accountability for the military leadership of Myanmar.

But as an expert in genocide and mass atrocity prevention, I believe the ruling goes far beyond these nations. Indeed, it is also a watershed moment for international legal justice that is bound to have important effects on the court’s other ongoing genocide cases, particularly the case of South Africa v. Israel .
Gambia’s case focused on actions that Myanmar’s military government called “clearance operations” in the course of its decades-long violent persecution of the country’s Muslim Rohingya minority .

The Tatmadaw , as the Myanmar military is known, justified these actions as a counterinsurgency operation. Yet in the course of those attacks, soldiers were found to have destroyed hundreds of Rohingya villages , and to have committed widespread rapes, torture and summary killings.

While the precise death toll of the 2017 attacks may never be known, at least 10,000 Rohingya civilians are thought to have died , and roughly 750,000 Rohingya fled to neighboring Bangladesh. There they joined other Rohingya in what is now the world’s largest refugee camp of over 1.2 million people, comprised of those who had already fled years of the Myanmar government’s persecution and attacks.

The court’s ruling that the Tatmadaw’s attacks amounted to genocide rested on its interpretation of the crime of genocide in the 1948 U.N. Genocide Convention , the first major international treaty approved by the United Nations General Assembly.

For an attack to be genocidal, it must be directed against an ethnic, religious, racial or national group, and must include at least one of five prohibited acts: killing members of a group; inflicting serious physical or mental harm on members; deliberately inflicting conditions calculated to bring about its destruction; imposing measures intended to prevent births; or forcibly transferring children from the group.
Beyond these factual requirements, genocide requires that the perpetrator specifically intended these acts to destroy the group, in whole or in part.

In its ruling, the court agreed that the facts of Myanmar’s attacks met the legal definition of genocide. For the notoriously difficult and demanding requirement for proving the “ special intent ” to destroy a group, the court determined that the pattern, selective targeting and lethality of the attacks on Rohingya villages could not plausibly be explained as a counterinsurgency operation.
Instead, the only reasonable inference that could be drawn from the military’s actions, the court determined, was the specific intent to destroy the Rohingya ethnic minority.
The court’s decision is unprecedented in many important respects.

In an influential previous ruling on violations of the Genocide Convention, in Bosnia and Herzegovina v. Serbia and Montenegro in 2007, the court found only that Serbia had not met its legal duty to prevent genocide by failing to use its influence to restrain the Bosnian Serb army in the Srebrenica massacre of 1995 .
In the Myanmar ruling, by contrast, the court ruled for the first time that a country is legally responsible for committing genocide – not merely failing to prevent it.

Further, the court ruled for the first time that a country that has committed genocide also has multiple obligations toward the victim group. Those include designing and implementing a comprehensive program of reparations and compensation for victims; creating conditions where Rohingya can make a safe, voluntary and dignified return to their homes; and restoration of their citizenship status after national legislation from 1982 rendered them stateless .

Finally, the court also demanded that Myanmar take steps to investigate all those involved in the genocide to determine individual criminal responsibility. Since the International Court of Justice is not a criminal court and only hears cases between states, this order explicitly connects the ruling to other courts where individual perpetrators can be held accountable.

These include the International Criminal Court – which had already requested an arrest warrant for Tatmadaw leader Min Aung Hlaing – as well as national courts that may pursue prosecution according to the doctrine of universal jurisdiction.
The court’s ruling in Gambia vs. Myanmar is also likely to have huge ramifications far beyond the case itself.

In filing its complaint, Gambia appealed to an innovative argument to establish that it had legal standing. It argued for what’s known as “ erga omnes partes ,” roughly translated as “toward all parties to a treaty.” According to this line of reasoning, the Genocide Convention imposes such strong legal duties to prevent and punish the crime of genocide that any state, even one that has not in any way been directly harmed, has the standing – in fact, the obligation – to seek legal remedies.

In accepting Gambia’s “erga omnes partes” approach, the court opened a pathway for other cases centering on violations of the Genocide Convention. Of these, the most significant by far is the ongoing case of South Africa v. Israel , which charges the Israeli government and the Israeli military of committing genocide against Palestinian civilians in the Gaza Strip. Going forward, other nations would now also have a legal tool for holding perpetrator states accountable for committing the most serious international crimes.

The International Court of Justice has no enforcement arm. As such, the Myanmar government cannot be compelled to abide by its rulings, whether to cease any further attacks or persecution on the Rohingya, make efforts to repatriate them or design a comprehensive reparation and compensation plan.

But even if Myanmar chooses to ignore the court’s specific orders, the ruling is a major defeat. The reputational damage of being the first country found guilty of state-sponsored genocide is likely to be considerable. Further, the ruling will support claims that other nations have a duty not to assist Myanmar in any way that might support or enable further attacks on Rohingya.

While that doesn’t automatically mean other countries will fulfill their duties under international law, many are nonetheless likely to use the ruling to bolster multilateral efforts to impose political, economic and social costs on the Tatmadaw. That could include targeted economic sanctions, financial restrictions, prohibitions on arms sales and other forms of cooperation with Myanmar’s government. The ruling thus comes with a potentially hefty price tag for the military junta.

Given the general weakening of international legal institutions over the past 20 years, a dysfunctional U.N. Security Council and an International Criminal Court under siege by the Trump administration , the court’s ruling is a rare victory for international justice and opens new routes for international genocide prevention and accountability efforts.
Before all else, though, it is also a victory for the Rohingya – a people who have suffered decades of persecution.

Thousands gathered in their Bangladeshi refugee camps to watch and cheer as the court’s president, Judge Iwasawa Yuji, read the court’s judgment. Camp inhabitants held aloft signs and chanted a simple message as the verdict came down: “Thank you Gambia.”

articles.title: US and Iran once practiced diplomacy through archaeology – that legacy need not lie in ruins
articles.author:
<name>Kyle Olson, Lecturer in Archaeology, Washington University in St. Louis</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/kyle-olson-2473957"/>
paras: When a U.S. airstrike struck Tehran’s Arg Square on March 2, 2026, Golestan Palace was not the target. But it was close enough.

The missile’s impact blew out windows across the palace complex and damaged some of its elaborate 19th-century interiors. In photographs taken afterward , pieces of its celebrated mirrorwork lay scattered across the floor.

Golestan is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the great surviving monuments of Iran’s Qajar dynasty, which ruled from 1789 until 1925. Within hours of the strike, UNESCO reported the damage and noted that cultural property is protected under international law during armed conflict.

The palace was not only an early casualty of the U.S.-Iran war, but a symbolically potent one, too. And as my colleague Mehrnoush Soroush at the Center for Ancient Middle Eastern Landscapes has documented , Golestan is not alone. Since the war in Iran began in February 2026, reports of damage to heritage sites have poured in from all across Iran.

I know that damaged buildings — no matter how valuable — cannot compare with the human costs of war. But the images from Golestan have particular resonance to me, an archaeologist who studies the history of relations between Iran and the United States . It also cuts against a history of cooperation between American and Iranian archaeologists, in which Americans worked to preserve, rather than destroy, Iranian heritage.
I have spent years researching how archaeologists, museums and cultural officials from the two countries worked together before the Iranian Revolution of 1979 .

My earlier research has examined how archaeology became entangled with American foreign aid and Iranian development programs during the 1960s, and I am currently writing a book on the history of U.S.-Iranian heritage diplomacy over the past century.

I believe that history offers another way of thinking about what has been lost in the current conflict. Long before Iran and the U.S. became adversaries, cultural heritage provided a setting in which people from the two countries learned how to work together.

American archaeologists began excavating in Iran in the early 1930s . In those days, the relationship was unequal: American museums sought access to archaeological sites and, under agreements with the Iranian government, received portions of the objects they excavated under the colonial system of partage . As a result, museums across the U.S. still hold substantial collections of Iranian antiquities.

The terms of the relationship changed considerably during the 1960s, as the U.S. and Iran intensified their connections. At the same time that thousands of American professionals, educators, businesspeople, scholars and others came to work and live in Iran, the country revised its antiquities laws and expanded its own archaeological institutions, universities and museums , resulting in, among other things, a major tourism boom .

American archaeologists still wanted permission to dig at Iranian sites, but they increasingly operated within a system controlled by Iranian officials. In return, American institutions contributed funding and access to laboratories, specialist knowledge, graduate education and connections to an international scholarly community.

American archaeological projects in Iran drew on large networks of such connections. Scholars working on the Deh Luran Plain in southwestern Iran, for example, depended on Iranian government agencies, the U.S. Embassy, American universities and museums, development organizations and scientific laboratories. Botanical remains, animal bones and other materials moved through specialist laboratories abroad, while Iranian officials worked alongside foreign researchers in the field.

By the 1970s, fieldwork projects were increasingly becoming joint enterprises, based on formal partnerships between institutions and cooperative leadership. Iranian archaeological authorities employed American specialists to help survey areas threatened by dams and other development projects , while Iranian archaeologists increasingly took leading roles in the field. Meanwhile, students moved in greater numbers between Tehran, Chicago, Philadelphia and New York. Museums organized traveling exhibitions , and Iran hosted international scholarly congresses devoted to its history and archaeology.
It can’t be ignored that these collaborations flourished during a period when Iran, under Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi, was a close American ally .

While the terms of the relationship increasingly favored Iran, they were still marked by geopolitical inequalities. American universities and museums possessed resources that Iranian institutions often lacked – not only financially and in terms of human capital, but physically, in the form of collections of artifacts that had previously been taken out of Iran.
Yet the collaborations also developed lives of their own, as American scholars returned year after year.

The Islamic Revolution exposed both how extensive and fragile this network was. Even as the crisis that began in 1978 deepened, American archaeologists did not initially assume that their Iranian partnerships were finished. At Malyan, the remains of ancient Anshan, archaeologist William Sumner proposed continuing to pay a watchman to protect the site, while maintaining contact with Iranian colleagues so research could eventually resume.

That did not come to pass. And much of the American-Iranian archaeological enterprise collapsed as diplomatic relations between the two countries soured after the Islamic Republic took 52 American diplomats and civilians hostage in 1979 and Washington sided with Baghdad during the Iran-Iraq War in the 1980s.
But the example of the 1960s and ‘70s points toward a sometimes less visible part of diplomacy: relationships accumulated through repeated practical work.

International relations expert Trita Parsi makes this point in his history of the negotiations that produced the 2015 Iran nuclear agreement . In “ Losing an Enemy ,” based on interviews with participants on both sides, Parsi describes the working relationship that developed between U.S. Secretary of State John Kerry and Iranian Foreign Minister Mohammad Javad Zarif.

This is not to say that their personal rapport produced the nuclear agreement by itself. Naturally, presidents had to authorize negotiations, diplomats at all levels had to find compromises, and both governments had to conclude that an agreement served their interests. But contemporary reporting described that relationship as one built on professional respect and repeated close proximity. In other words, Kerry and Zarif spent enough time negotiating together to understand each other’s constraints and establish a working relationship despite the hostility between their two governments.

That kind of personal working relationship can assist diplomacy – not just at the highest levels but more broadly across civil society. Sports diplomacy has long been acknowledged; so too the sharing of zoological “gifts.” My research shows that archaeology has long had an important a place in these kinds of cultural exchanges as well.
Today, Iranian conservation specialists are sorting and cataloging shattered fragments from Golestan Palace while attempting to repair damage at heritage sites around the country .

At the same time, American and Iranian officials are still looking for ways to end the conflict. I don’t know what U.S.-Iranian relations will look like when the fighting eventually ends, but damaged buildings and monuments will need to be repaired and conserved. If my inbox is anything to go by, Iranian scholars still want to work together with American colleagues.
And if a larger political opening for U.S.-Iranian rapprochement ever arrives, the relationships built by those who steward and study Iran’s heritage may matter more than they first appear.

articles.title: Nvidia isn’t the first company to dump a misbehaving CEO – history shows it’s in the interest of corporate boards to act
articles.author:
<name>Michael Nalick, Assistant Professor of Management, University of Denver</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/michael-nalick-2487414"/>
paras: The story may sound familiar: The CEO of one of the largest and most powerful tech companies resigns over sexual misconduct allegations. The move causes the company’s stock to drop by more than 10%, wiping out billions in value. It also raises scrutiny of the company’s board of directors and whether it made the right decisions ahead of the crisis.
This could easily describe the turmoil facing Nvidia after the ouster of its CEO , Jensen Huang. But it actually transpired over 15 years ago at Hewlett Packard, under CEO Mark Hurd.

Jensen Huang is just the latest in a long line of CEOs who lost their jobs over personal misconduct. And as with HP, scrutiny is shifting from his behavior to his board – and the decisions that led to his exit.

Prominent industry leaders are questioning the board’s decision to oust him. They include Peter Steinberger of OpenAI, Anduril Industries co-founder Palmer Luckey, Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan. Meanwhile, an internal petition allegedly signed by more than 1,600 Nvidia employees has also called for Jensen Huang’s reinstatement.

As a scholar of management who has researched corporate misconduct, I believe the board made the right call. After collecting instances of CEO personal misconduct dating back to 1995, I have repeatedly found that doing nothing, as a board, is worse than doing something.

CEO personal misconduct isn’t simply a private matter or an isolated leadership failure. I believe it creates reputational and governance risks for directors and can embolden further misconduct when left unaddressed. It may also signal deeper problems within the organization.
But it’s still hard for boards to act, particularly when the CEO is also the company’s founder and a central figure in its success. If the board is earning billions , it’s even more difficult.

One important change over the years is that boards are becoming more sensitive to misconduct matters due to greater scrutiny by the media and public. They’re also more aware of the consequences for their own job that stem from the board’s performance and entanglement in the misconduct. In fact, directors of companies whose CEOs are involved in personal misconduct exit at a significantly higher rate than normal, either because they choose to leave a messy situation or because they’re forced out due to poor performance, my research shows.

One of the better known examples is Best Buy founder Richard Schulze, who stepped down as chairman of the board in 2012 after an internal investigation revealed that he knew about former CEO Brian Dunn’s inappropriate personal relationship with a female employee and failed to report it.

Directors are also personally penalized for their association with their company’s corporate misconduct. They may lose their board seats or see other companies they’re associated with take a hit. And if they hold executive positions elsewhere, the misconduct may spill over to damage the reputations of those companies as well.
In other words, directors have a rational basis to be concerned about their reputations and how a CEO’s personal misconduct may tarnish it.

In the case of Nvidia, questions are now being asked about the rigor of board oversight, the lack of CEO succession planning, and whether the board knew anything about the affairs. These questions have now spread to issues of potential national security risks .

Another issue is moral hazard : when someone acts recklessly because they know someone else will bear the cost if things go wrong. Assuming individual directors do face penalties for CEO personal misconduct, they have to address the likelihood of incentivizing further misconduct if the CEO is retained, which would further stain their reputation.
My research has found that risk to be high.

When CEOs are caught engaging in misconduct and the board doesn’t act, it can create a moral-hazard precedent and emboldens the CEO to behave badly again. In fact, when CEOs engage in repeated personal misconduct, the second instance is often even worse than the first.

Take former American Airlines CEO Doug Parker, who was the subject of two publicly reported DUI arrests. The second incident, in 2007, attracted considerably more media attention while prompting criticism of the board for allegedly failing to disclose the first incident in 1991.

Christopher Kubasik is another example of a second chance gone wrong. He was recently ousted as CEO of defense contractor L3Harris Technologies, more than 14 years after being forced out of Lockheed Martin following allegations of similar personal misconduct involving an inappropriate relationship.

In the case of Nvidia, Jensen reportedly lied to company officials about the nature of his intimate relationships for more than a year. From the board’s perspective, if he lied about this, what else has he lied about? And if they let him off the hook, what would he lie about in the future?
Broader, often uncomfortable questions about company culture are also at stake.

CEO personal misconduct can be a symptom of a larger cultural problem at the company, my research shows. And it’s often associated with other types of corporate misconduct that affect the very operations of a business. In fact, other types of corporate misconduct frequently occur around a similar time frame as the personal misconduct of an executive.

Take Dov Charney’s tenure as CEO of American Apparel. During his leadership, the company faced significant accounting problems in 2009-10 that required it to re-audit several years of financial statements. Around the same time, Charney faced multiple allegations of personal misconduct, including sexual harassment, sexual assault, racist remarks and abusive behavior toward employees.

It’s in boards’ interest to grasp that personal misconduct can indicate a larger organizational issue – and, as a result, lead to more scrutiny of the board. With Nvidia, for example, there’s now a spotlight on the company’s organizational culture, its financial dealings and its possible role in skirting U.S. sanctions on Chinese chip import restrictions. The board is likely looking at the totality of the issues and not just the personal misconduct.

For now, the public debate has largely centered on what the company might lose without Jensen Huang at the helm. An equally important question, though, is what the company and its board might risk by retaining a CEO whose conduct has raised serious questions about judgment, trust and organizational oversight.

It’s a board’s duty to protect its organization from managers who go astray, as legendary investor Warren Buffett noted : “It isn’t fundamental dishonesty that causes people to go in a different direction. It’s human nature. There are plenty of people who are really decent people, intelligent people. … But they just don’t come to grips with reality. And boards usually don’t push them to.”

articles.title: Eurovision took its song contest to Asia – bringing its political drama and cultural tropes along for the ride
articles.author:
<name>Paul David Flood, Assistant Professor of Musicology, University of Tennessee</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/paul-david-flood-2762688"/>
paras: ABBA and Céline Dion came to the world’s attention thanks to the Eurovision Song Contest, an annual showcase of pop music, camp and spectacle.

Filipino singer Carmelle is hoping that the Eurovision Song Contest Asia will serve as a similar springboard to international fame. On Nov. 14, 2026, Carmelle bested entries from 11 Asian countries to be crowned the Asian edition’s first-ever winner . The competition marked Eurovision’s boldest expansion of its format in its 70-year history.

As a scholar of contemporary European popular music and politics , I study the ways in which Eurovision shapes notions of what it looks like and sounds like to be European. Knowing that the Asian edition would be organized by European broadcasting executives, I wanted to see how closely Eurovision Asia would resemble the flagship Eurovision, or whether it would carve out an identity of its own.

Eurovision’s proposed expansion into Asia dates back to 2008, when the European Broadcasting Union – the transnational coalition of public service media organizations that has organized the Eurovision Song Contest since 1956 – announced plans for “ Our Sound – The Asia-Pacific Song Contest .” Originally slated to debut in 2010, the project never materialized.

On March 31, 2026, however, Voxovation, a European-led production company that oversees the development of Eurovision’s spinoffs, announced that Bangkok would host the inaugural Asian competition in partnership with Thailand’s Channel 3 and S2O Productions.
Eurovision Asia is now the second European Broadcasting Union-licensed global spinoff to make the airwaves.
In 2022, Voxovation organized the American Song Contest , which included original songs by artists from all 50 U.S. states, five territories and Washington.

Despite being promoted to the American public in a Super Bowl commercial featuring hosts Kelly Clarkson and Snoop Dogg, the competition failed to attract a large viewership and the spinoff wasn’t renewed.

Given two decades of uncertainty, as well as the failure of Voxovation’s U.S. spinoff, some critics doubted whether the Asian version would succeed. And for a moment, it looked like everything might fall apart: In late October 2026, the Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet reported that Eurovision Asia’s original budget of approximately US$4.5 million had been reduced by US$1 million.

The European Broadcasting Union, however, confirmed that the show would go on as planned, and at 8:30 p.m. Bangkok time on Nov. 14, the show’s two hosts, Thai media personalities Woody Milintachinda and Cindy Bishop, welcomed viewers from around the world tuning in via television broadcast and the YouTube livestream.
“Maybe you’ve never heard of Eurovision before, or maybe you’re one of the hardcore Eurofans,” said Bishop. “It doesn’t matter, because you will be blown away by the talent here tonight!”
For the next two-and-a-half hours, each country’s representative performed an original song, with Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên opening the show with her song “Em Tiên” (“Fairy Maiden”).

Vietnam’s entry had many of the spectacular ingredients of an ideal Eurovision entry: bilingual lyrics, large props, flashy outfits and a dance break. The song’s instrumentation included a flute accompanying Tiên’s melody and a bamboo xylophone. It concluded with a second, high-energy dance break reminiscent of electronic dance music genres.

The song’s use of traditional Asian musical signifiers followed the approach of the European entrants that have incorporated folk traditions to promote their national cultures to an international audience.

For example, Ukraine’s 2004 winning entry, Ruslana’s “ Wild Dances ,” opened with the trembita , a long alpine horn associated with the Hutsul people of the Carpathian Mountains. Armenia’s 2008 entry, Sirusho’s “ Qele, Qele ,” similarly combined a traditional Armenian duduk flute , zurna trumpet and dhol drums with an upbeat dance track and contemporary pop vocals. While some scholars claim that these musical gestures strategically romanticize and exoticize regional cultures , it’s a way to fuse national identity with modern music.

Other Eurovision Asia entrants also pulled from this playbook. Mongolia’s singer, Beck, wore a deel , the country’s traditional robe, while performing . He also incorporated a traditional Mongolian string instrument into his performance.

Voting, which was open to the general public via an online form, began just before the first performance. Viewers were allotted eight free votes, on the condition that they had to vote for at least three different countries . They could purchase 10 additional votes. The public accounted for half the votes, while a jury made up of representatives from each nation accounted for the other half.

Carmelle’s winning song – a Filipina women’s empowerment anthem titled “Sobra-Sobra” (“Too Much”) – featured a repeated musical line played by a kulintang , a Filipino percussion instrument, and a frenetic dance break. The song’s bridge was rapped in Tagalog , the country’s national language.
As part of her reward, Carmelle will perform “Sobra-Sobra” at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Burgas, Bulgaria.
No Eurovision competition would be complete without a measure of political controversy.

From broadcaster boycotts over Israel’s participation amid the war in Gaza to suspicions that Franco’s Spain rigged the 1968 Eurovision vote in its favor , political disputes have long been part of the competition.

Normally, political statements are not permitted in Eurovision , though exceptions have been made for humanitarian causes. Ukraine’s victory in Eurovision 2022 took place just a few months after Russia’s full-scale invasion of the former Soviet republic. Oleh Psiuk, the frontman of Ukraine’s entrant, Kalush Orchestra, pleaded for support for Ukraine at the end of the performance, which the European Broadcasting Union ended up allowing.
During Eurovision Song Contest Asia, Malaysia found itself at the center of controversy.

Malaysian entrant Aina Abdul, who wears a hijab in her public appearances, performed her song “Bluest Sky.” While Abdul was seen as a possible favorite, Malaysian audiences claimed that she ultimately did not score enough points due to Islamophobia .

Another controversy arose due to the Malaysian broadcaster TV3’s coverage of the show. During the results segment at the end of the show, the camera feed of the Filipino spokesperson, the drag queen Vice Ganda, was cut from the Malaysian broadcast. Malaysian broadcasting laws restrict the airing of drag and LGBTQ+ content on television, radio and digital platforms.
In a comment to The Guardian , Eurovision Director Martin Green said, “We are surprised and disappointed to learn that the broadcast of Eurovision Song Contest Asia was altered in Malaysia.”
“We take this matter seriously and will be writing to Voxovation,” Green added.

Here, there are also echoes of the European competition: Eurovision has embraced multicultural and pro-LGBTQ+ values to such an extent that countries like Hungary and Turkey have withdrawn due to their governments’ incompatible sociopolitical values.
Eurovision Asia’s controversies prove that the European Broadcasting Union has a new – perhaps unexpected – set of geopolitical and sociopolitical values to navigate.

Television viewership for Eurovision Asia varied by market. In Vietnam , the show reached over 5 million viewers. The host country’s broadcast , however, only reached an average of 385,000 Thai viewers. These numbers pale in comparison to Eurovision 2026’s viewership of 131 million viewers across the 35 competing nations.

Nonetheless, hype is already building for the 2027 edition of Eurovision Asia. During a news conference in Bangkok, Voxovation executive Christer Björkman confirmed that multiple cities have expressed interest in hosting, with China, Japan and Taiwan indicating that they’re open to participating in the future.

If more Asian broadcasters buy in, Eurovision will attract an even larger international audience, bringing Voxovation one step closer to turning the contest from a European tradition into a global phenomenon.
But time will tell whether Eurovision Asia can become something more than a European competition staged elsewhere.

articles.title: Google acquires Seattle startup Howie and its AI scheduling assistant
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Google is bringing Seattle-based Howie , maker of an AI scheduling assistant that works from your inbox, into its Google Labs division.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed this week. Google Labs, the company’s experimental arm, announced the acquisition in a post on X , saying it “can’t wait to learn from them as we build the next generation of intuitive AI tools together for small businesses.”

Howie CEO and co-founder Austin Petersmith said on LinkedIn that the team will continue building Howie at Google. “Howie has always been built on top of Gmail and Google Calendar, so Google Labs is the perfect place for us to take this product to the next level,” he wrote.

Petersmith co-founded Howie around 2023 with CTO Dave Newman . The two first worked together in 2013 at Assembly, which Newman co-founded, and prototyped an AI assistant in 2015 before deciding the market wasn’t ready.

Users cc Howie on an email thread, and it coordinates meeting times, adds events to calendars, follows up as needed and flags scheduling conflicts. Customers set their own rules in an open-ended preferences document, such as “if it’s a pitch call, set it to 25 minutes and use Zoom.”
Behind the scenes, Howie ran tasks through fine-tuned language models and looped in human scheduling experts when the AI wasn’t confident.

Howie raised a $6 million seed round led by True Ventures in September 2025, when it launched publicly out of private beta. At the time, it had more than 1,000 paying customers, including startup founders, venture capitalists, recruiters, consultants and journalists, and was scheduling more than 5,000 meetings a week.

The deal comes as Google and rivals including OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta race to build AI agents that complete tasks on behalf of users. Google Labs acquired music generation platform ProducerAI earlier this year .

articles.title: Pinehurst Station Posts Anemic Ridership in First Full Month
articles.author: Doug Trumm
paras: After Sound Transit inaugurated service on September 30, the Pinehurst infill light rail station in North Seattle averaged a measly 1,034 daily boardings in October, according to the agency's ridership dashboard . That makes it the least used station in the entire 1 Line corridor.

The initial figure is below even the low-end ridership modeling that Sound Transit produced, which showed Pinehurst would attract 2,600 to 4,200 boardings daily by the year 2040. Granted, Pinehurst has 14 years to hit its 2040 projection, but it does have a long way to go.

The busiest station, Westlake, averaged more than 17,000 daily boardings in October, and the entire corridor saw just over 155,000 daily boardings across 27 stations. The median 1 Line station has averaged about 4,000 daily boardings.

Pinehurst's October ridership did exceed seven of the 12 stations that serve only the 2 Line, which has also struggled to build ridership momentum on the Eastside. Bellevue's East Main is the least used light rail station in the entire system, with just 487 daily boardings last month.

Pinehurst is sandwiched between two far more popular stations. Northgate averaged nearly 7,500 daily boardings in October, while Shoreline South (just north of Pinehurst) averaged more than 3,600 daily boardings.

Pinehurst is last among 27 stations on the 1 Line – at least so far. A number of transit advocates warned the station's ridership potential was at risk, as the Harrell administration dragged its feet and ran into legal appeal hurdles as it attempted to rezone the neighborhood surrounding the station.

Rezoning the golf-course-oriented, largely single family neighborhood to encourage apartment development has been part of the pitch for Pinehurst Station from the inception of the grassroots campaign that willed the station into existence. While the station has been funded since the 2016 Sound Transit 3 (ST3) ballot measure, the rezones have been mired in the Seattle Process .
Sound Transit CEO recently appeared on KUOW's Soundside program and was interviewed by David Kroman and Libby Denkmann. They brought up the issue of low ridership at Pinehurst Station.

"Both Libby and I actually ride past the station a few times a week. I have to admit we have made a little bit of a game of counting how many people actually get on and off there," Kroman said. "I think we would both agree that it has been pretty sparse, as far as we can tell. You know, when you look out [from the train], all you really see is I-5, a few single-family homes, a golf course. Do you think more could have been done here, both by the City of Seattle and Sound Transit, to prepare for that station to open?"
Constantine did not take the bait, hewing to a 'if you build it, they will come' line for the station, which carried a budget of $240 million.

"Well, I think, along the way, there are stations with a lot of built-in ridership and stations with less ridership that are about mobility for the people who live close," Constantine said. "And some of those stations with less ridership become centers for growth later, right? And I think this is going to be one of those stations."
The agency CEO alluded to the Pinehurst rezone plan working its way through the process, as he noted some other station areas have transitioned from sparsely populated to dense and bustling.

"The City of Seattle is looking at their growth plans around there, their zoning around there, the incentives they can provide around there for people to create housing," Constantine said. "If you look at our stations up and down the line, our new stations, you see apartment buildings, condominiums going up all over the place by the thousands, and that will happen at Pinehurst as well. So I'm absolutely confident that we're going to see increased ridership at that and other similarly situated stations over time."

At the ribbon-cutting ceremony for Pinehurst, Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson echoed Constantine's optimism, which acknowledging the delay and expressing resolve to see the rezones though, which she has also sought to augment with her Taller Faster Denser Plan .

"This is not just a station; it is a spark – a spark for long-term transformation in the newly designated Pinehurst-Haller Lake Urban Center, where we will see more homes, shops, services, parks, and walkable streets, all connected to great transit. That's what it's all about," Wilson said. "Sometimes we build transit where lots of density already exists, and sometimes we build transit, and we're able to welcome people around them."

Constantine and Wilson could have a point based on the path some other stations took. Shoreline South managed just 1,020 daily boardings in its first full month of service – very similar to Pinehurst – but it's more than tripled ridership in the two years since. Shoreline North and Mountlake Terrace took a similar course of steady ridership growth. (On the other hand, Lynnwood City Center's ridership has fluctuated widely, but its level is now similar to when it launched, hovering around the 4,000 daily riders mark.)

That said, ridership growth at each of those locations was buoyed by fairly ambitious upzones that had been put in place before the stations opened, which allowed large apartment complexes to come online near the station opening date. Seattle, on the other hand, is playing catch up after pushing the agency to accelerate the infill station opening, while failing to keep rezone plans on course, despite facing some pressure to do so.

In 2023, former Kenmore Councilmember and Sound Transit Board Member Dave Baker criticized Seattle for not rezoning the Pinehurst neighborhood sooner as Mayor Bruce Harrell and other City officials pushed the agency to accelerate the station's opening.

“I’m sorry Mayor Harrell, I’m not trying to throw stones, but it’s just reality that they’ve had the opportunity to increase zoning in the area to make it more transit-friendly, but it’s still not done,” Baker said. “They’ve had since 2015 to fix the zoning, and it’s now 2023 and the zoning has still not been fixed. I would love to see a successful station… and the system to be as functional as it can. Everything else seems to be happening except this one.”

Harrell brushed off the comment and spent the next few years failing to keep his growth plan on schedule or to insulate it from legal appeals, while undercutting his planning department's more ambitious vision.

After kicking around more meager concepts, the City ultimately queued up a rezone for the Pinehurst-Haller Lake Urban Center allowing five- to eight-story apartment buildings and ground-floor retail in several swaths of Pinehurst and some more limited areas of Haller Lake, replacing some broad areas of low-density Neighborhood Residential (NR) zoning. Other NR areas are set to become Lowrise 1 or 2, which would likely be most enticing to townhome builders, based on recent development patterns.

Across the new urban center, OPCD projected its boldest "Alternative 5" rezone would generate about 2,700 additional homes over 20 years. Meanwhile, the City has projected anemic growth without zoning changes, with just 840 additional homes expected over two decades.

Harrell and his predecessor Jenny Durkan also opposed changes to publicly-owned Jackson Park Golf Course, which advocates had proposed could attract more usage if it incorporated other park uses (or even housing ) – instead of remaining exclusively a fenced, fee-for-entry 27-hole golf course. As it stands, the golf course consumes 160 acres next door to the station, interrupting more direct walking routes to reach it.

If the Pinehurst rezone had not been yoked to the City's broader once-per-decade Comprehensive Plan major update, it might have already happened. However, at the time, City officials seemed to deem it expeditious and convenient to piggyback on the outreach and feedback process for the citywide plan, which they originally set out to pass by the end of 2024 to meet state deadlines.
Pinehurst-based organizer Renee Staton, who fought to add the infill station in the first place, said support for rezones has long been strong in the neighborhood.

"There is substantial community support for a rezone and unlike other communities in Seattle, there is no formal opposition effort to rezoning. In fact, many residents are frustrated with how long the station area planning process is taking, considering it started in 2015," Staton wrote in a guest piece in The Urbanist in September.

Staton has pushed Seattle political leaders and officials at the City's Office of Planning and Community Development (OPCD) to complete the rezone work as soon as possible. Alas, 2028 might be the best case scenario.

"I spoke with OPCD on Monday and they are very optimistic that the One Seattle rezone process will start again in mid-2027 (which I hear as early 2028 given budget season and elections). Pinehurst rezone 2028," Staton added in a social media post last week.

Even if zoning were to be put into place, large apartment complexes often take three years or more to go from a permit application to a completed building, assuming builder interest is immediate – which isn't always guaranteed in a neighborhood more or less starting from scratch on urban development. The broader One Seattle rezones will include opening up many other areas of the city, with some more amenity-rich areas likely more attractive to builders.
In other words, significant amounts of development likely won't be arriving in Pinehurst until the 2030s. A botched neighborhood growth plan can be rectified, but it does take time.

articles.title: Seattle Council and Mayor Spar Over Amended Budget
articles.author: Amy Sundberg
paras: The Seattle City Council finalized 2027-2028 budget legislation, weighing amendments Friday and Monday in a two-day marathon that felt at times like it might go off the rails. Throughout, the process highlighted clear tensions between councilmembers as they argued about transparency and fiscal responsibility under the pressure of a ticking clock.

The meetings culminated in a close 4-5 vote on a piece of legislation sponsored by Councilmember Dionne Foster that would have required council to exercise the same fiscal responsibility they had just voted to continue to require of Seattle’s mayor.

Council President Joy Hollingsworth and Councilmembers Bob Kettle, Maritza Rivera, Rob Saka, and Dan Strauss voted against Foster’s bill. The legislation would have required that the council’s ongoing spending not exceed ongoing revenue, a measure that would help prevent future deficits.

“As we passed the balancing requirement for the mayor last year, I think it's important that we are not holding ourselves to a different standard, or to say differently, if a standard is good enough to ask that we are requesting that another branch of government meet it, I believe it's fair that we ask ourselves to fall in line with that same standard,” Foster said.
In their comments before the vote, councilmembers appeared to tie themselves into rhetorical knots trying to express their commitment to fiscal responsibility while voting explicitly against it.
“I don't need a law to do what's right in this situation,” Strauss said. “I don't need a law to tell or an executive order to tell me how to do my job well.”

Strauss went on to complain that the Mayor’s Office has five months to develop their budget proposal whereas the Budget Chair only has five weeks to create the balancing package, a timeline that predates Strauss’s tenure as Budget Chair.

“As council, we need flexibility,” Saka said. “Again, we are the final check on the Executive as this legislative branch, and I think this ordinance, great in intent and purpose in terms of being sustainable – and I support those broader goals – I also think it would voluntarily restrict one of our most sacred constitutional and charter level responsibilities: deciding how public dollars are spent.”
Kettle agreed that flexibility was paramount, above fiscal responsibility.
“We are a co-equal branch, but we are in a disadvantaged position,” Kettle argued.

“I just want to be clear: it is not that I don't want to hold us accountable to ensuring we have balanced budgets years out, but it takes a certain kind of fiscal responsibility that, as I said earlier, I have not seen in council in many years in order to do that. And part of that, at least for this year's budget, this police piece, I'm sorry, the fire piece was really important to do,” Rivera said.

The council could have chosen to include ongoing funding for the Seattle Fire Department’s (SFD) overtime in their budget proposal instead of one-time funds, but that would have required that they make other difficult choices, which they largely chose to avoid.
Hollingsworth opted not to share her reasons behind her “no” vote.

Central Staff’s explanation, in response to a question from Lin about flexibility, that the legislation wouldn’t preclude the council from exercising discretion when necessary didn’t appear to convince councilmembers who were opposed.
Most of the councilmembers who voted against the bill originally ran on platforms calling for fiscal responsibility and budget audits in 2023.

“I am supportive of Councilmember Foster’s bill that would have held the Council to the same standard of fiscal responsibility as the mayor,” Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson said in a statement. “While it didn’t pass out of committee, I sincerely hope the Council takes it up again later this week.”
All legislation considered on Monday will receive another vote at the special Full Council meeting on Friday, November 20.
Last Friday’s meeting included two executive sessions, whereas Monday’s meeting lasted for ten-and-a-half hours and included a last-minute presentation from the council’s Central Staff.

While the council’s budget process is always a bit rushed, Budget Chair Dan Strauss scheduled the final budget vote on November 20 instead of the traditional Tuesday before Thanksgiving, peeling away a few valuable days of discussion and error-checking. This year, holding the vote on November 24 would have added the complication of interim Councilmember Debora Juarez losing her voting power as soon as local officials certify election results that day, with Councilmember-Elect Nilu Jenks taking over when that happens. Unlike Juarez, Jenks is expected to vote with the progressive bloc, generally speaking.

Meanwhile, Strauss’s balancing package , introduced at the beginning of November, included new investments and new revenue sources that councilmembers barely had time to learn about and discuss. Strauss’s original intent was to vote on all budget amendments and legislation on Friday alone, significantly curtailing any chance for councilmembers to debate the merits of the proposals, but he was thwarted when a lawsuit filed by the Seattle Firefighters Pension Board required the council to have two substantial executive sessions to discuss the legal ramifications of the budget policies on which they were voting.

In spite of this setback, councilmembers ended up voting yes on most of the budget amendments before them, adding even more spending – most of it one-time – to a balancing package that had already added more than $40 million to Wilson’s original budget proposal. Even Strauss’s proposal to add $150,000 for Ballard holiday lighting and a lit-up Jimothy decoration was approved, albeit by a close vote. Strauss is a long-time Ballard resident.

City Budget Director Aly Pennucci sent a letter to council on November 6, warning them of the pitfalls ahead. While Pennucci praised Strauss for presenting a balancing package that didn’t present a deficit in 2029, she cautioned councilmembers that including so many supposedly “one-time” adds in the budget could easily knock the budget back into deficit territory in the future. Pennucci identified many one-time adds in the balancing package that had originally been requested as ongoing, calculating that those items being included as ongoing expenses instead would have led to a $21.5 million deficit in 2029. If all the one-time adds for 2027 became ongoing commitments, that would lead to a $41 million deficit.

“I heard clearly from many of you over the last two months that you consider ending one-time funding as a ‘budget cut.’ So, I want to be clear with you, City employees, and community partners, that items labeled as ‘one-time’ in the budget for 2027, 2028, or both, will be removed from the 2028 and/or 2029 baseline budget,” Pennucci wrote.

During Monday’s budget meeting, a week and a half after receiving this communication, Councilmember Maritza Rivera said she saw one-time budget adds as a way to potentially prove they should become ongoing.

“Sometimes that means proposing one-time funding with the understanding that that funding might not be ongoing, and we need to hold ourselves accountable for that,” Rivera said. “The hope is that the mayor sees the value of the investments that we include, and that that funding is made ongoing if needed. And of course, there's no guarantees that the mayor will do that.”
Pennucci also warned about Strauss’s diversion of $10 million from the JumpStart reserve, saying if the council didn’t change course, a new reserve policy would need to be developed next year.

“The stated intent of the JumpStart reserve is to protect JumpStart investments against future economic uncertainty, not to fund new Council priorities as it has been used two of the last three years,” Pennucci wrote.

Councilmembers also expressed concern about the adoption of a 0.01% children and families sales tax that was passed by King County earlier this year. Strauss proposed the City take their share of the tax, although he hasn’t developed a long-term spending plan for the usage of this new revenue. In addition, there was a lack of clarity around impacts this action would have on King County’s plans for the money.
“I can't speak fully to what those impacts might be at this time,” said Pennucci.
After Monday’s votes, Wilson released a statement on the council’s budget proposal, pointing out the one-time funding issue.

“The proposal that passed the Select Budget Committee increases spending from the General Fund by a net of $36 million in 2027, $31 million of which is one-time,” Wilson wrote. “ This means that there is over $20 million of Council-proposed spending in 2027 that is not funded in 2028. ” [Emphasis original]
There were a few notable budget amendments and pieces of legislation that did not pass council’s scrutiny, bucking the trend of layering on commitments.

Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck’s proviso on $400,000 in the Seattle Police Department (SPD) until the department implements the three recommendations from the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) regarding their surveillance program was rejected with a 3-6 vote, with Foster and Councilmember Eddie Lin joining Rinck in voting yes.

“I do want to take this opportunity to just say on the record that Axon and Flock are one and the same,” Rinck said just before the vote. “They're companies that have their roots with one another. They have a deep and long history, but they started together. And I don't want us to think that we're necessarily choosing the lesser of two evils. I know Flock has gotten a lot more bad press with the challenges of their system. It's important to note that Axon has a fair share of their own challenges and in fact holds a nearly $32 million contract with ICE.”

In a moment of inadvertent humor before the vote, Saka said he trusted the Mayor’s judgment on this issue. Councilmembers have been overtly critical of Wilson and her judgment for many months, particularly on her decision to pause their surveillance expansion – before she ultimately greenlit it this month after further study.

Strauss’s proviso on $2.5 million of the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) to support bus service on routes 15 and 17 in outer Ballard failed with a 4-5 vote, probably partially motivated by the fact that Route 15 no longer exists and can’t be brought back without a vote from the King County Council.

Finally, Foster’s legislation that would have created a designated fund if and when the City is able to recover the $13.1 million SPD mistakenly paid to its employees earlier this year didn’t receive enough support. The fund would have put aside any recovered funds for affordable housing instead of returning them directly to the General Fund.
Both Saka and Strauss insisted on verbal amendments to Foster’s bill, but even after she agreed to these changes, Strauss abstained, knowing this would mean the bill wouldn’t pass with a 4-4 vote.

Councilmembers had a sudden budget policy decision to make when the Seattle Firefighters Pension Board filed a lawsuit against the City on November 10, as reported by PubliCola . The Board objected to Wilson’s proposal in her budget to eliminate the actuarial account and transfer all of its funds to the statutory pension fund. Wilson had proposed using $10 million of that money for 2027-2028, thus freeing up General Fund money for other purposes.

In his balancing package, Strauss proposed using an additional $22 million of that money over the biennium, freeing up even more General Fund dollars and using up most of the money transferred from the actuarial account, making this another one-time budget fix.

articles.title: Op-Ed: Microsoft’s PAC Failed, but Governor Ferguson Is Still Coming to Heel
articles.author: John Burbank (Guest Contributor)
paras: Two weeks ago, after the blue tsunami buried Trump’s legions and his megacorporate allies, Governor Bob Ferguson convened a session of his newly established Economic Development Council. This wasn’t about taking advantage of this wide-open moment of political opportunity to advance policies for working people in our state. Instead of proposing how to make child care and healthcare affordable and to halt the polarization of wealth and income to the already wealthy and powerful, Ferguson simply signed an executive order to stop all new state regulation of corporate Washington .

The governor was applauded by Brad Smith, President of Microsoft, and Rachel Smith, President of the Washington Roundtable , an advocacy group for big business. It was all smiles at the press conference, but a giveaway to corporate Washington is meaningless to the citizens of our state.

In Washington DC, Microsoft has committed $10 million to Trump’s ballroom and the destruction of the East Wing of the White House, plus another $1 million to his inauguration which featured oligarchs including Elon Musk and Jeff Bezos, among other anti-patriots.
Was it worth it for Microsoft? Yes. Microsoft received a $144.4 million contract in January from the U.S. Air Force.

Likewise, Amazon has made out well thanks to Trump, with their donation of $5 million for the Ballroom. Amazon Web Services won a Department of Homeland Security cloud contract in June worth up to about $2.6 billion . That’s a return on investment of 52,000%, while Microsoft’s is a measly 1,444%! These corporations are not our friends – they are Trump’s lieutenants for the oligarchy.

Microsoft seems to think it can get away with looking like it is a good corporate citizen, all while building a new political action committee, Washington Needs to Compete . Washington Needs to Compete has nothing to do with competing, but instead focuses on making sure corporate politicians stay in power. Microsoft failed this year. But this PAC has now raised almost $14 million in anticipation of 2027 and 2028 political battles.
They may think they are rich and strategic, but our 2026 election results indicate that they may just be angry about the anti-Trump wave and trying to figure out a way to create an undertow for MAGA.

Washington Needs to Compete spent over $1.7 million to defeat progressive Democrats. But these Democrats prevailed in 5 out of 6 races. In Kitsap County, Washington Needs to Compete spent almost $300,000 to try to defeat Rep. Tarra Simmons, a formerly incarcerated person who worked her way up from prison to law school to becoming an attorney and defending the rights of incarcerated Washingtonians, and who happens to be the best state legislator in running House floor sessions. Simmons won.

Washington Needs to Compete spent over $700,000 to defend Rep. Amy Walen, a car dealer Democrat, who has represented the 48th LD, which is located in the Eastside suburbs and includes Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters. She lost to a progressive Democrat by 5%. While Walen voted against the millionaires tax, her replacement Jessica Forsythe has pledged to support it.

Yes, Washington needs to compete. We need to make our state a place in which workers, including high tech workers and doctors and nurses and professors, want to stay and raise their families. That means we need to compete, not with Alabama, but with Canada.

What makes Canada so great? For a family it is all about making ends meet and thriving. In Canada the parents of a newborn are entitled to over one year of financial support , to enable that infant to be cared for by her parents. In Canada, through government funding, child care costs $10 a day and it is universal. In Washington, child care costs parents ten times as much . In Canada, there are no out-of-pocket costs and no premium for medical services coverage .
At the University of British Columbia, one year of tuition is $6,200 . At the University of Washington, one year of tuition is $14,000 .

Thinking about health care, child care, family leave, and tuition for higher education, there are all sorts of reasons for workers, including highly skilled professionals, to leave Washington state and move north. And they have.

From March 2025 until January 2026, British Columbia received more than 2,750 job applications from U.S. doctors, nurse practitioners, nurses and allied health professionals. British Columbia has been aggressively recruiting from our state.
Last summer, former Governor Christine Gregoire asserted that the state government has a spending problem . But the reality for working people is that we have a paucity problem.

We have consistently cut back higher education, child care compensation, K-12 education, and care for developmentally disabled Washingtonians, just to name a few. These should be and in previous decades were fully funded as public goods and services.

Indeed, Washington needs to compete – not with Alabama and those states and policies still corrupted by Jim Crow and deep and persistent racism, but with 21st century democracies like those in the Nordic countries and just north of us. We don’t need to accelerate the undermining of the working class and further fatten the portfolios of the already wealthy. These wealthy elite have no loyalty to our state. Just ask Jeff Bezos and Howard Schultz.

articles.title: Neighbors told Kaiser Permanente to re-activate its empty storefronts — Now Emma Cakes is bringing a walk-up bake shop to 15th Ave E
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A new walk-up bakery is set to bring fresh life to a long-vacant retail bay along 15th Ave E at Kaiser Permanente’s Capitol Hill campus.

The City of Seattle has issued a construction permit for the tenant improvement buildout of Emma Cakes inside the 440-square-foot storefront at the corner of 15th Ave E and Denny. Rather than operating as a sit-down cafe, the interior will function as a commercial kitchen dedicated to cake production and baking, paired with walk-up service on the sidewalk. Architectural plans call for modifying a front window panel just left of the main entrance to install a self-closing, bifold pickup window.

The storefront marks a brick-and-mortar expansion for baker Emma Lavine , founder of the Normandy Park-born custom cake business. In a 2024 interview , Lavine shared that she began baking as a creative outlet during the pandemic while studying Studio Arts at San Diego State University . After posting cakes on Instagram for fun, demand from friends and classmates turned the hobby into a side hustle. Following graduation, she formed a company and launched the business professionally, crediting the disciplined, early-morning work ethic she learned watching her father run his own company.
The streamlined footprint is engineered to keep construction and operating overhead low, avoiding major structural and mechanical upgrades typical of a full-service installation.

Until now, Lavine has operated as a one-woman show out of Normandy Park, pitching her custom cakes as edible art for celebrations, ranging from 6-inch two-layer “mini” cakes to 9-inch “extra-large” cakes, alongside add-on cupcakes and pastries. The new storefront gives her a dedicated Capitol Hill cake production facility alongside a street-facing walk-up counter.
The arrival also represents progress in Kaiser Permanente’s push to activate its quiet 15th Ave E streetfront.

As CHS reported in fall 2025 , retail spaces along the block sat empty for years following the pandemic, drawing scrutiny from the citizen Implementation Advisory Committee that oversees the city’s 2018 Major Institution Master Plan for the former Group Health campus.

In response to neighborhood calls to meet its street-activation requirements, Kaiser Permanente brought on hospital retail specialist Health Hospitality Partners and launched a community survey to help shape new food, coffee, and retail offerings.

Commercial listings for the Capitol Hill South Building’s street-level spaces along 15th Ave E show brokers marketing remaining adjacent bays at $28.00 to $30.00 per square foot per year, plus a share of building taxes, insurance, and maintenance.
For now, Emma Cakes is leading the way but there are hopes for more activity to come.
In the meantime, the coming shop will add to this stretch of 15th Ave E’s baked good-ness, joining the nearby location of Bakery Nouveau in serving Capitol Hill’s sweet tooth.
Emma Cakes will open soon at 104 15th Ave E. Learn more at emmacakesseattle.com .

articles.title: Alternative Transit Modes
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: As I explained in an earlier guideway post, Sound Transit chose light rail technology to make it easier to use the existing transit tunnel and to run and stop at grade but many new technologies have been developed since. As Sound Transit builds a lot more elevated and tunneled sections and opens new lines in urban areas, it may need to reevaluate that decision. Sound Transit and Metro already use buses, heavy rail (for Sounder), ferries, and trams. Other cities like San Francisco, Mexico, and Paris use even more different modes like people movers and gondolas. In that post I talked about monorail and maglev guiderail systems. They are easier and faster to build due to prefabricated guideways, are slicker and therefore visually less obtrusive, and may offer easier maintenance.

As Sound Transit is facing escalating construction costs and feels it cannot accommodate traditional elevated trains downtown, it may be a good time to evaluate these and other alternative transit modes. Monorail systems have opened in Bangkok, and TSB has built a maglev test line in China and is looking at several options in Germany. Swyft Cities (working with Whoosh Solutions) and Ottobahn are working on cabins which hang from a guideway like the Wuppertaler Schwebebahn and provide personal rapid transit (PRT).

Similar to a Waymo or Zoox robotaxi, Swyft Cities and Ottobahn offer more route flexibility, are called via phone app, and have small individual cabins with an electric motor. Unlike a robotaxi, they use airspace and don’t get stuck in traffic, they are confined to its track network, have specific parking/staging areas, use electric motors with track power, and use small stations. While Swyft cabins travel on fixed cables (similar to a gondola or the RopeTaxi but those are propelled by the cable), Ottobahn cabins travel on regular tracks at 37mph. For longer distances Ottobahn claims up to 150mph. Both use track switches to guide cabins to their destination.

Ottobahn cabins hang off a bogie which is powered by an electric motor with regular wheels and steel tracks. Cabins either stop at elevated stations or can employ a lift mechanism which drops the cabin to the sidewalk for on- and off-boarding. Ottobahn claims they can support 6000 riders per hour in each direction, or even more with a favorable network design. Similar to a monorail, their track is supported by towers about 120ft apart and between 15 and 30ft high. The track can also cross longer distances over rivers and other obstacles akin to a suspension bridge. Cabins can usually climb up to 7%, with extra support even 12%. That may allow a ship canal crossing.
Swyft is hoping to start projects in Queenstown, Miami, or Los Angeles. Ottobahn started construction of its first network in Phuket .

Traditional train lines serve stations along a linear corridor. Turning a train around at the end of the line takes time as the operator usually has to switch from one end of the train to the other. Lines may branch towards the outer area of a network, but that splits the headway on each branch. As automated train systems do not need to worry about a driver, they can switch direction more easily and offer a bit more flexibility. For example, they can serve short stub lines by backing in and out, though that may impact travel time. PRT systems are not bound to any fixed line/schedule, can use a more elaborate track network, branch on demand, skip stations, and only stop as necessary. Though each cabin may be smaller, short headways may still allow for sufficient capacity.

Any of these systems promise simpler/faster guideway and station construction, easier integration into the existing urban infrastructure, more flexible branching capabilities, and more convenience for riders. It may be worthwhile to consider them for West Seattle or Ballard and other future lines.

articles.title: Maintenance of automated trains
articles.author: Martin Pagel
paras: Sound Transit has recently reduced construction cost with smaller station designs (for example Alaska Junction) but their current four-car trains are 380ft long while Vancouver’s SkyTrains are only 280ft long. That still requires bigger, harder to locate, and more expensive stations. Due to automation SkyTrain can operate more frequently and therefore still handle higher ridership while providing higher convenience. Sound Transit has considered automation but is concerned about interoperability with current trains. They could add an operator on surface portions such as through Rainier Valley. If they would keep the Ballard line separate, then interoperability would not be an issue, but Sound Transit would need to worry about where to park them at night (“stabling”), clean them, and maintain them. When Sound Transit considered a starter line for Ballard, they concluded that they would need to build an operations and maintenance facility (OMF) in Interbay and that its cost would offset all savings. I gathered some ideas on how to potentially reduce such effort.

If you connect the Ballard (starter) line with the main line, you could still use the existing Central OMF in SODO. If such a connection is not feasible, then you could build a separate regular OMF or consider other options.

For maintenance, you could connect to the BNSF tracks at Interbay and SODO to move trains between the Ballard line and the SODO OMF during off-hours. As BNSF tracks are not electrified, you would need a separate locomotive to pull the trains. You could also truck the trains as these occasional maintenance events.
For nightly cleaning and monthly maintenance, you may still want a separate small cleaning center just like SeaTac airport cleans their people movers locally.

When Lynnwood Link opened, Sound Transit did not have enough stabling space at the Central OMF. They parked some trains at various stations at night . Operators had to pick them up there in the morning and park them there at night. Automated trains may operate through the night. If you do not want to operate through the night to maintain the tracks, you can park automated trains anywhere. They can wake themselves up in the morning, go through safety checks, and move to the first station by themselves. In fact, if Sound Transit wants to reduce service in the evening and start cleaning cars, they could send them to the OMF for daily cleaning and afterwards park them at any pocket track. If they want to reduce service further, they even reduce service to a single track towards the end of the line and use the other track for stabling.
This would reduce the size and cost of the OMF considerably. As automated trains can move (“shunting”) themselves in and out of the OMF, there is no need for shunting staff.
Sound Transit could even allow construction of transit-oriented housing above such facility as the Hong Kong MTA has done for example.
If Ballard trains don’t need to use the Central OMF in SODO, Sound Transit may be able to reduce the size of the Everett OMF. This may shift some of the cost.

I would hope by reducing the cost of the maintenance facility, Sound Transit would consider an automated Ballard starter line and shorter stations. Due to its lower cost, it could connect Ballard sooner and also be more attractive to riders due to its higher frequency and longer service hours.

articles.author: <name>Mark DeJoy</name>
paras: The University District is frequently (and wrongly) written off as a place only college kids would want to eat; the story usually goes that it’s rife with sketchy lunch counters, nondescript multinational fast food chains, and an overabundance of boba tea joints. But the truth is that the U District is one of the city’s essential dining destinations, with a dizzying array of global cuisines concentrated on its main street, University Way (confusingly known as the Ave).

There’s Korean food, regional Chinese specialties, Indian groceries, Vietnamese kitchens, falafel windows, and more on nearly every block. And practically everything is both affordable and genuinely good, so figuring out where to eat in this neighborhood is more a matter of grappling with the paradox of choice than anything else. articles.title: Cafe Lolo Is the Neighborhood Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves
articles.author: <name>Kat Thompson</name>
paras: If I were to describe the perfect neighborhood restaurant, Cafe Lolo would completely fit my definition. The food is comforting and nourishing, emphasizing local ingredients, which playfully come together in a way that feels both fresh and familiar. The space is draped in natural light that’s assisted by over a dozen lamps. The inviting dining room is covered in quirky Renaissance-inspired murals that don’t feel disruptive. There are to-go meal kits available for purchase, as well as local beers. It’s an atmosphere that invites you to unwind with a bottle of wine. Owners Leah Engel, Alex Halmi, and Brett Bankson are present, not only flitting about the room, but also cooking the dishes in the kitchen and laughing with customers. If I lived in the neighborhood, just off the main drag of Capitol Hill, it’s somewhere I’d want to return to over and over again.

Cafe Lolo has an extensive wine menu and many local beers, as well as bottles in the fridge you can pick up to-go. Although yes, the wine list — which includes just one glass from Washington, and more options from Oregon and Europe) — is worth perusing, the nonalcoholic tisanes are also made from seasonal ingredients. The strawberry rhubarb soda I had on my visit was effervescent and floral without an overpowering sweetness.

Like the rest of the menu, dessert will change pending seasons — but don’t skip it. My visit included a celebration of ripe, macerated strawberries over a semolina olive oil cake, which had a buttery crust and a tender interior crumb. There was also a scoop of rhubarb sorbet; light, sweet, and sharp.
